instructions.text: Trim, scrape, or singe off any hairs or bristles. Cut out the eyes.
Remove ears, brains, snout, tongue, or jowls if using separately; otherwise leave on for grinding.
Halve or quarter the head with an axe. Soak overnight in fresh water to remove blood.
Rinse until water runs clear.
Put in a pot of clean, salty water and cook slowly until meat falls off the bones.
Remove all meat from bones and run through a food chopper.
Season with sage, red pepper, black pepper, and salt to taste.
Mix thoroughly and put into jars, a mold, or a plate covered with clean white cloth.
Store in smokehouse where winter weather will keep it fresh.

notes: Can be eaten cold or reheated
Ears are gristly and leave white flukes in the meat - some find this unattractive
Alternative seasoning: one onion, one pod strong red pepper chopped fine, one tsp salt
Beulah Perry uses: red and black pepper, onion, a little corn meal, sage and garlic
Evie Carpenter adds: a little vinegar, sage, black pepper and onion

recipes.title: Scrapple
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book, as told by Mrs. Mann Norton
recipes.description: Cornmeal mush with hog's head meat. Mann Norton added, 'Just hold your tongue so y'didn't swaller it when y'went t'eatin'!'

instructions.text: Take the head, take the eyeballs out and the ears, and cut down in there. Get all the hairs off.
Put it in a big pot and cook it til the meat just turns loose of the main big bone.
Lift them bones out, and lay your meat over and feel with your hands to check for bones.
Strain your liquid through a strainer so the little bones come out.
Put the liquid back in a pot, and put that mashed meat back in that liquid.
Put your sage and pepper in there.
Stir it til it got to boiling.
Stir in plain corn meal til it's just plumb thick.
Pour it up in a mold, and cut it off and fry it and brown it.

notes: Mrs. Norton: 'Tastes just like fish.'

recipes.title: Liver Pudding (Liver Mush)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian hog recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Traditional liver mush made with hog liver and cornmeal.

instructions.text: Cut up the liver, wash it well, and remove skin.
Boil until tender in salted water.
Remove and run through a colander until fine, or mash well.
Mix the meat with one cup of the broth it was cooked in.
Bring to a boil slowly, stirring in sifted corn meal until thick.
Stir in salt (to taste), half teaspoon black pepper, two tablespoons sage, and a little red pepper if desired.
Pour into a mold and let sit until cold.
Slice and eat. Some eat it as a sandwich, or warm the slices in bacon fat.

notes: Can be eaten cold, as sandwich, or warmed in bacon fat

recipes.title: Mountain Sausage
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian hog recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Traditional country sausage with sage and peppers, preserved in hot grease.

instructions.text: Use any combination of lean meat not used otherwise - trimmings from hams, shoulders, middlin' meat, tenderloin, head meat, and jowls if desired.
Run the mixture through a sausage grinder.
Fry it good and brown (but not completely cooked since it has to be reheated when served).
Pack into jars (half to three-quarters full) while still very hot.
Pour hot grease over the top.
Close the jars and turn them upside down to cool.
When the grease cools, it seals the lids shut.

notes: Store with jars remaining upside down
Many parch their own red pepper in front of the fireplace, crush it, then add to sausage
Alternative storage: Roll into balls, pack in churn jar, pour hot grease over, tie cloth over lid, set in spring house water trough
Can also pack in cleaned small intestine, tie off, hang in smokehouse
Or pack in washed corn shuck, tie closed, hang in smokehouse
Or pack in small clean white cloth sacks and hang in smokehouse

recipes.title: Chitterlings (Chitlins)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian hog recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Fried hog intestines - a traditional mountain delicacy.

instructions.text: Put sections of intestine in a jar of salt water and let sit for three or four days.
Take out, rinse, wash, and rinse again.
In winter, can lightly salt, put in jars, and keep a few days before cooking.
When cooking, cut up in small pieces and remove any unwanted layers of lining.
Boil in salt water with a half pod of pepper until tender.
Either dip into a batter made of flour, water, and baking powder (with an egg if desired) and fry; or roll in corn meal and fry in grease.

recipes.title: Watermelon Pickles
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Sweet pickled watermelon rind.

ingredients.prep_note: pink pulp and outer peel removed

instructions.text: Remove all pink pulp from watermelon rind. Peel outside peeling from the rind. Weigh.
Cut in 1 inch circles or cubes.
Combine cold water and lime. Pour over rind. Let stand one hour. Drain.
Cover with fresh cold water. Simmer 1 1/2 hours or until tender. Drain.
Tie spices in a cheesecloth.
Combine vinegar, 1 quart water, and sugar. Heat until sugar dissolves.
Add spice bag and rind; simmer gently two hours.
Pack rind in clean hot sterile jars. Fill jars with boiling hot syrup. Seal.

recipes.title: Tomato Catsup
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Homemade tomato ketchup.

ingredients.unit: enough to make a gallon when cooked

instructions.text: Select good, firm ripe tomatoes.
Scald and strain through a coarse sieve to remove seed and skin.
When cold, add to each gallon of tomatoes the spices, sugar, vinegar, and salt.
Let simmer slowly for three hours.
Seal in bottles or jars.

recipes.title: Pear Preserves
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Simple pear preserves with sugar.

instructions.text: Wash pears, peel, and cut into quarters. Rinse.
Place a layer of sugar and a layer of pears until all the fruit has been used.
Let this stand overnight.
Put over moderate heat and cook until well done and a syrup has been made from the mixture.
Put into sterile jars and seal.

recipes.title: Mint Jelly from Apple Juice
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Apple-based mint jelly.

instructions.text: Pour boiling water over the clean mint leaves.
Cover and allow to steep for one hour.
Press juice from the leaves.
Add 2 tablespoons of this extract to 1 cup apple juice and 3/4 cup sugar.
Boil until jelly test is reached.
Add green food coloring.
Pour into hot glasses and seal.

recipes.title: Muscadine Wine
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Traditional muscadine grape wine.

instructions.text: Mash the grapes with your hands.
Put them in a large churn and add 2 1/2 pounds sugar.
Let it work (ferment) for about a week, until it quits.
Strain the mixture to get out the grape skins and impurities.
Put back in the churn, add 10 pounds more of sugar.
Let it work about eight to ten days until it quits.

recipes.title: Apple Beer
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: A simple fermented beverage made from apple peelings.

ingredients.prep_note: dried in sun or by stove

instructions.text: Peel your apples and dry the peelings in the sun or by the stove.
Put them in a crock and add enough boiling water to cover them.
Cover the crock and let it sit for one or two days, until all the flavor comes out of the peelings.
You may add some sugar if you want.

notes: A frugal way to use apple peelings that would otherwise be discarded

recipes.title: Fried Squirrel
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian wild game recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Pan-fried squirrel - a mountain hunting tradition.

ingredients.prep_note: skinned, gutted, soaked to remove blood

instructions.text: Soak the squirrel long enough to get all the blood out.
Cut into pieces.
Roll the pieces in flour, salt, and pepper.
Fry until tender and brown.

notes: If the squirrel is old, you may want to parboil it in water containing sage to take out the wild taste
Can also make squirrel dumplings: parboil 5 min, cook in fresh water until tender, add pepper, butter, milk to broth, drop in dumpling dough and cook 10 min covered

recipes.title: Fried or Baked Rabbit
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian wild game recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Mountain-style rabbit prepared by frying or baking.

instructions.text: Cut the rabbit into sections. Remove the legs, and separate the ribs and back section by cutting up the rabbit's sides vertically.
Parboil the pieces in covered pot in salted (two tablespoons) water to make tender if not young.
For frying: put the parboiled pieces in a greased pan and fry until brown on all sides, seasoning with half teaspoon pepper. Some roll pieces in meal or flour before frying.
For baking: dip parboiled pieces in a breaded solution of two eggs, four tablespoons flour, quarter cup milk, and half teaspoon pepper. Bake until brown (about thirty minutes).

notes: Can also be simmered in salted water until tender and served as is

recipes.title: Possum and Sweet Potatoes
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian wild game recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Classic mountain possum baked with sweet potatoes. Beulah Perry loved the possum head as a child.

ingredients.prep_note: scalded, scraped, gutted, musk glands removed

instructions.text: Scald the possum in boiling water containing a half cup of lime or ashes.
Scrape until hairless, gut (should have been bled immediately after caught).
Remove the musk glands under the forearms, and either the head or at least the eyes.
Soak overnight before cooking.
Parboil in water containing salt and red or black pepper to taste until tender.
Put in a greased pan surrounded or filled with sweet potatoes.
Bake until golden brown (about two hours if using a wood stove).

notes: Beulah Perry: 'Lot a times, when I was a kid, the possum head was my favorite... You eat the tongue, brains, everything in the head except the eyes.'
Alternative: line pan with sassafras sticks instead of grease
Can also skin possum, parboil until tender, cut up, roll in pepper and flour, and fry

recipes.title: Baked Raccoon
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian wild game recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Raccoon baked until golden brown - a mountain hunting tradition.

ingredients.prep_note: skinned, musk glands removed, gutted, soaked

instructions.text: Skin the coon, remove the two pear-shaped musk glands from under the forearms.
Gut, remove head, tail, and feet. Soak overnight in cold water to get the blood out.
Put in a pot of salted water (one spoon of salt per pound), one or two pods of red pepper or one tablespoon of black pepper.
Boil with no lid until the meat is tender.
Remove, put in a greased baking pan, and bake until golden brown.

notes: To remove wild taste: add spicewood twigs, an onion or two, a teaspoon of vinegar, or some potatoes to parboiling water
Alternative: parboil, rub with salt and pepper, dot with butter, add quartered sweet potatoes around meat, bake at 400°F until tender
Can also parboil, cut into pieces, roll in corn meal, and fry in lard
Can be salted and smoked like ham for later use

recipes.title: Baked Groundhog
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian wild game recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Groundhog baked until brown.

ingredients.prep_note: about the size of a baby's fist, optional

instructions.text: Skin the groundhog, remove the glands from under the legs, gut, and soak overnight in salty water.
Parboil with spicewood twigs (to take the wild taste out) until tender.
Pepper and put in a greased pan to bake until brown.

notes: The hide was often placed in a bucket of ashes over which water was poured. After the ashes took the hair off, the hide was dried, kneaded, and cut up in strips for shoe strings.
Alternative: parboil until tender in water with two carrots, garlic, and a piece of fat meat about the size of a baby's fist, add pepper and 1 tbsp salt. Then brown in open baking pan.
Can be dried, salted, and smoked for later use

recipes.title: Venison Stew
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian wild game recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Hearty venison stew with vegetables.

instructions.text: Cut two pounds of meat into one-inch cubes and brown on all sides in a small amount of fat.
In a stewing pot, add the meat, two cups water, four potatoes, six large carrots, four medium onions, one quart of tomatoes, one tablespoon salt, and one teaspoon pepper.
Bring to a boil and simmer for three hours.
After three hours, thicken with three tablespoons flour and one half cup water.
Eat then, or store in a cool place and heat as needed.

notes: Alternative thickening: flour, three tablespoons bacon drippings, and a pint of tomato juice

recipes.title: Venison Loaf
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian wild game recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Meatloaf made with venison and pork.

instructions.text: Mix together ground deer meat, ground hog meat, eggs, salt, pepper, chopped onion, and dampened breadcrumbs.
Shape into a loaf.
Bake for about an hour at 400°F.

recipes.title: Fried Turtle
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Battered and fried turtle meat.

instructions.text: Clean turtle: chop head off, drop shell and all into boiling water, cut meat loose from shell, gut, cut into pieces.
Soak meat overnight in salty water (some add a little soda) to remove the wild, strong taste.
Parboil if desired (with salt and hot pepper).
Cool and dip meat into a batter made of one cup plain sifted flour, one half teaspoon salt, one teaspoon baking powder, two beaten eggs, and one half cup milk.
Fry in deep fat until golden brown.

notes: Alternative: parboil, roll in flour, and fry with 3 tbsp flour, 1 tbsp salt, 1 tsp pepper in covered skillet
Can also stew in sweet milk and butter, pepper and salt just like oyster stew

recipes.title: Fried Frog Legs
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book, as told by Mrs. Lake Stiles
recipes.description: Fried frog legs, as told by Mrs. Lake Stiles.

instructions.text: Get them dressed - cut the legs off and clean them and throw the rest away.
Get your grease not too awfully hot - if you get it too hot, when you put the legs in they'll jump out.
Roll them in flour and salt and pepper like chicken, and fry them.
Or you can take buttermilk and an egg and whip it together, then roll the legs in it and either bread crumbs or cracker crumbs, and fry.

notes: Mrs. Lake Stiles: 'Get your grease not too awfully hot - if you get it too hot, when you put the legs in they'll jump out.'

recipes.title: Ash Cakes
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Corn bread baked in hot ashes - the original mountain bread.

instructions.text: Mix up dough for corn bread, and make sure it's thick enough to hold its shape.
Clean out a corner of the fireplace.
Put the 'cake' in it and cover it with a clean cloth.
Put hot ashes over the cloth, then put hot coals on top of that.
It takes about half an hour.

notes: The original way to bake bread in the mountains

recipes.title: Bran Bread
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Hearty bread made with bran flour, raisins, and molasses.

instructions.text: Mix together bran flour, white flour, and buttermilk.
Add seeded raisins and molasses.
Last mix in baking soda and salt.
Put into loaf pans and bake until done.

recipes.title: Rye Bread (Biscuit Style)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Quick rye bread cut like biscuits.

instructions.text: Sift together wheat flour, rye flour, corn meal, salt, and baking powder.
Add enough buttermilk to make a firm dough, adding 1/2 tsp of soda per cup of buttermilk.
Cut in shortening, mix thoroughly.
Roll out to about 1/2 inch thick.
Cut as you would biscuits, place on greased sheet.
Bake at 450°F for ten to twelve minutes.

recipes.title: Molasses Cookies
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Simple molasses cookies.

instructions.text: Mix brown sugar, egg, molasses, melted lard or butter, boiling water, and salt.
Add enough flour to knead.
Roll, cut out, and bake in hot oven.

recipes.title: Homemade Butter
recipes.source_note: Traditional butter churning from The Foxfire Book
recipes.description: Traditional churned butter with tips for proper temperature and handling.

instructions.text: Fill churn half or slightly over half full with rich milk which should be mostly cream.
Set the churn aside so the cream can 'turn' or clabber. In summer, pour up one night and churn the next. In winter, warm on alternate sides by fireplace for 3 days.
Test readiness: tilt the churn to its side - liquid should hold together in one form, separating cleanly from sides.
Insert dasher into churn, cover with lid (hole in center for dasher stick).
Agitate up and down for 30-40 minutes until butter gathers.
Remove lid and stir gently with the dasher in a sideways motion to bring butter together.
Lift lumps of butter out, drain, place in bowl.
Either chill overnight in refrigerator then mold with salt; or rinse with cold water immediately for fresher flavor.
Press butter into mold. Store in cool place.

notes: If clabbered cream is too warm: result is soft white puffy butter - add cold water to improve texture
If too cold: yields specks that won't stick together - stir in hot water to help gather
If left too long, cream will curdle and separate and won't make good butter
If churned too early while still 'blinky milk,' won't make good butter either
Liquid left after butter removed is buttermilk
Traditional chant: 'Come butter come, Come butter come, Peter standing at the gate, Waiting for a butter cake, Come butter come.'

recipes.title: Sassafras Tea
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian spring tonic from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A spring tonic tea made from sassafras roots. As they say, 'Drink sassafras during March, and you won't need a doctor all year.'

instructions.text: Find a small bush, pull up roots and all, or dig down by the base of a tree and cut off a few sections of root.
Wash the roots and scrub until the bark is pink and clean. Peel off the pinkish bark for tea.
Put one cup shredded bark in quart of boiling water.
Boil ten to twelve minutes.
Sweeten with sugar to taste. Can be served hot or with ice.

notes: Sassafras is best gathered in spring when the bark 'slips' or peels off easily
Red sassafras is considered best but hard to find nowadays
Big roots should be pounded to a pulp before boiling

recipes.title: Sassafras Jelly
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A unique jelly made from strong sassafras tea.

instructions.text: Boil two cups strong sassafras tea and one package powdered pectin.
Add three cups strained honey.
Strain and put in jars.

recipes.title: Dock Greens
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian wild greens from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Young dock leaves cooked as greens, rich in vitamins A and C. Dock greens eaten in spring will thin and purify the blood.

instructions.text: Wash dock leaves thoroughly.
Parboil until leaves turn a lighter green.
Pour off water, wash two or three times.
Either fry in hot grease and salt for three to five minutes, or bring to a boil in fresh water, season and serve.

notes: Often cooked in combination with horseradish, mustard, or turnip greens
Cooked with meat, dock leaves are said to make the meat cook more rapidly

recipes.title: Hot Greens on Toast
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Creamy dock greens served on toast with bacon.

instructions.text: To one pint of cooked dock, add one tablespoon chopped onion, two tablespoons horseradish, and one cup sour cream or a little vinegar.
Season with salt and pepper.
Serve on toast and top with fried bacon.

recipes.title: Dock Soup
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian soup from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A creamy soup made from young dock leaves.

instructions.text: Cook young leaves, drain off water and strain.
Add milk, onion, butter, and two tablespoons flour.
Cook slowly one-half hour.

recipes.title: Sorrel Soup
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A rich, creamy soup from sheep sorrel leaves, high in vitamin C.

instructions.text: Chop sorrel and onion together (or ramps, if available).
Simmer in butter until wilted.
Add eggs and cream.
Bring to a quick boil and serve.

notes: Ramps can be substituted for onion if available

recipes.title: Sorrel Omelet
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A fresh omelet made with wild sorrel leaves.

instructions.text: Wash and dry young sorrel leaves. Chop fine.
Add to eggs, with some onion.
Cook omelet.
When omelet is cooked, sprinkle more fresh sorrel leaves on top.

recipes.title: Rhubarb Pie
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A layered rhubarb pie with biscuits, served cold with milk or cream.

instructions.text: Cut rhubarb stalks just above ground. Slice into half-inch pieces.
Cook with a little water over low heat in uncovered pan, stirring often, until rhubarb is the consistency of applesauce.
Sweeten with honey or syrup.
Layer in large flat-bottomed pan with half inch of rhubarb sauce, layer of split biscuits, layer of rhubarb, etc., finishing with layer of biscuits.
Chill and eat with milk or cream.

notes: Rhubarb leaves are poisonous - use only the stalks

recipes.title: Rhubarb Jelly
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A tangy jelly made from fresh rhubarb.

instructions.text: Wash and slice three pounds rhubarb.
Add one cup water and bring to a boil.
Reduce heat and simmer ten minutes.
Strain through cheesecloth.
Add three pounds of sugar (about seven cups) and bring to a rolling boil.
Add one bottle liquid pectin.
Cook, stirring, one more minute.
Pour in glasses. Jelly should harden in three to four hours.

recipes.title: Turk's Delight (Fried Rhubarb Flowers)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Battered and fried rhubarb flowers, dipped in sugar.

instructions.text: Gather rhubarb flowers.
Soak one-half hour in salt water.
Drain and dry.
Dip in batter and fry in hot fat.
Drain.
Dip in sugar and eat hot.

recipes.title: Poke Greens
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: The most popular wild food in the mountain area. Dr. Neville said to eat at least one mess of poke each spring - 'worth all the medicine you could buy.'

instructions.text: Collect tender young shoots of poke six to eight inches high in the spring. Do not cut below surface of ground as root is poisonous.
Wash and cook leaves and stems together, parboiling two times (pouring off water each time after boiling a few minutes).
Boil in third water until tender, salting to taste.
Drain and top with slices of hard-boiled egg.

notes: NEVER eat poke raw - it must be cooked
Roots and berries are poisonous
Avoid when stems become red and plant is over a foot high
Rich in iron and vitamin C

recipes.title: Poke Sallet
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Classic poke sallet fried with eggs.

instructions.text: Put greens in a boiler of cold water; wash two or three times.
Drain off all the water.
Fry in pan of hot grease. Add half teaspoon of salt.
Let cool. Beat two eggs and stir in after greens have cooled.
Serve with vinegar or pickle juice.

notes: Always parboil poke twice before frying

recipes.title: Poke Pickles
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian pickles from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Pickled young poke stalks, preserved in spiced vinegar.

instructions.text: Collect very young stalks, scrape, remove leaves, and pack in jars.
Combine one cup vinegar, half cup sugar, one tablespoon salt, one stick cinnamon, several whole cloves.
Boil, pour over poke, and seal.

recipes.title: Lamb's Quarter Greens
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Wild spinach-like greens. As someone said, 'If they think it's spinach, they think it's good.' Rich in iron and potassium.

ingredients.prep_note: streak of fat and streak of lean

instructions.text: Gather one gallon greens (lamb's quarters and dock).
Wash and boil for ten minutes.
Drain and add one cup water and four tablespoons grease.
Cook covered until tender.
If preferred, cook with a streak of fat and streak of lean.

notes: Can use white sauce with lemon, butter, bacon bits and vinegar instead

recipes.title: Pussley Casserole
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian casserole from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A baked casserole made from purslane (pussley), rich in vitamin C.

instructions.text: Cook purslane, drain, and chop fine.
Add eggs and cracker crumbs, or crumbled cornbread.
Bake.
Top with grated cheese just before serving.

notes: Can add bread crumbs, onion, poke greens, and beaten egg instead

recipes.title: Pickled Pussley
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian pickles from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Pickled purslane tips in mustard vinegar.

instructions.text: Cook wild onions with vinegar and one-quarter cup ground mustard seed.
Simmer, strain.
Pour over pussley tips.

recipes.title: Cress Salad
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian salad from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A fresh salad using wild water cress.

instructions.text: Toss together lightly: two cups finely cut cresses, one-fourth teaspoon salt, one tablespoon salad oil, one tablespoon vinegar, one tablespoon French dressing.

notes: Can also chop and add hard-boiled egg

recipes.title: Nettle Soup
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian soup from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A nutritious soup made from stinging nettles. Must gather with stout gloves!

ingredients.prep_note: gathered in early spring with gloves

instructions.text: Gather plants in early spring with stout gloves.
Cook a long time to destroy sting.
Add water, thicken with butter, flour, and egg yolks.

notes: Must gather with stout gloves
Repeated cookings destroy the sting

recipes.title: Baked Nettles
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian recipe from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Nettles baked with ground beef and rice.

instructions.text: Cook nettles a long time.
Strain off liquid.
Chop fine.
Add ground beef, rice, and seasoning.
Bake at low heat until firm.

recipes.title: Horseradish Sauce
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian sauce from The Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A classic horseradish sauce for beef.

instructions.text: Combine three tablespoons butter, one tablespoon flour, one and one-half cups boiling beef stock and horseradish to taste.
Cook until thickened and serve.

notes: Eating horseradish is said to be good for rheumatism, scurvy, and hoarseness

recipes.title: Mulberry Candy
recipes.description: Simple candy balls made from mulberries and walnuts.

instructions.text: Crush mulberries and mix with ground walnuts.
Make small balls and roll in sugar.

notes: Red mulberries ripen in June and are best for cooking

recipes.title: Mulberry Pie
recipes.description: A creamy pie made with fresh mulberries.

instructions.text: Cook mulberries and drain.
Mix with two beaten eggs, one cup cream, and 1/2 cup sugar.
Fill a pie shell and bake.

recipes.title: Serviceberry Pie
recipes.description: A pie made from serviceberries (sarviceberries). Jake Waldroop said, 'The berries are just wonderful for pies.'

instructions.text: Heat one pint ripe berries and 2/3 cup sugar.
Pour into a pie shell.
Bake in a hot oven.

notes: Serviceberries can be substituted for blueberries in pie recipes
Also called sarviceberry, juneberry, or sarvis

recipes.title: Serviceberry Flan
recipes.description: A custard flan with serviceberries.

instructions.text: Beat milk, sugar, flour, salt, and vanilla until smooth.
Pour half of the mixture into a buttered baking dish and bake one minute.
Add the berries, then cover with the other half of the mix.
Bake until set.

recipes.title: Dewberry Frosting
recipes.description: A bright frosting made from dewberry juice.

instructions.text: Cook berries and strain.
Use one cup juice to one cup confectioners sugar.
Spread on cake.

recipes.title: Dewberry Pie
recipes.description: A simple dewberry pie with a buttery top.

instructions.text: Mix one cup sugar, 1/4 cup flour, and dash of salt.
Fill a pastry shell with dewberries.
Sprinkle the mixture of sugar, flour, and salt over the top.
Dot with butter and bake.

recipes.title: Blackberry Cobbler (Foxfire 3)
recipes.description: Classic mountain blackberry cobbler with biscuit topping.

instructions.text: Cook the blackberries until they come to a boil.
Add the sugar, then some butter, and cook until thick.
Roll out the dough, cut as for biscuits, and drop into the blackberries.
Roll some dough very thin, cut it into strips and place on top of the blackberries.
Bake until the crust on top is brown.

notes: Blackberries were sometimes dried on strips of chestnut bark and stored in sacks

recipes.title: Blackberry Syrup
recipes.description: A spiced blackberry syrup for pancakes.

instructions.text: Mix all ingredients together.
Boil for fifteen minutes.
Use over pancakes.

recipes.title: Blackberry Flummery
recipes.description: A chilled blackberry pudding thickened with cornstarch.

instructions.text: Mix berries with water, sugar, salt, and cinnamon, and cook to the boiling point.
Reduce heat and cook slowly until liquid begins to look slightly syrupy.
Make a paste of cornstarch and three tablespoons water.
Stir into berry mixture, cook until slightly thick.
Serve cold.

recipes.title: Blackberry Roll
recipes.description: A rolled pastry filled with blackberries and honey.

instructions.text: Roll dough to 1/3-inch thickness, and brush with melted butter.
Combine 1/2 the berries with cinnamon and honey and spread them over dough.
Roll as a jelly roll. Place in a large, well-greased pan.
Surround with remaining blackberries and sugar.
Bake at 425° for thirty minutes.
Slice and serve from the pan.

recipes.title: Blackberry Jelly
recipes.description: Simple blackberry jelly made without commercial pectin.

instructions.text: Crush one quart berries in a pan without sugar or water.
Cook slowly eight minutes.
Strain; measure; bring to boiling point.
Add 1 1/2 cups sugar to each cup juice gradually, so the boiling does not stop.
Bring to a brisk boil, skim, and bottle.

notes: No commercial pectin needed - natural pectin in berries

recipes.title: Jake Waldroop's Blackberry Wine
recipes.description: Jake Waldroop's recipe for homemade blackberry wine, stored in an earthenware jug with a corn cob stopper.

instructions.text: Gather six to eight gallons of wild blackberries, wash them well, and put them in a big container.
Mix in five pounds of sugar.
Cover the top of the churn or container with a cloth, tied down so air can get in but insects can't.
Let the mixture work for eight to ten days.
Strain the mixture through a clean cloth, squeezing the pulp so that all the juice is removed.
Measure the juice you have. For every gallon of juice, add one and a half pounds of sugar.
Let it work off. When it stops (when the foaming and bubbling have stopped on top), strain it again.
Measure the juice, and again add one and a half pounds of sugar to each gallon of juice.
When it finishes working this time, it is done and can be bottled.

notes: Jake keeps his in an earthenware jug with a corn cob stopper
Makes grape wine the same way

recipes.title: Blackberry Cordial
recipes.description: A spiced blackberry cordial with whiskey.

instructions.text: Boil the berries until they will break into pieces.
Strain through a bag.
To each pint of juice, add one pound of white sugar, a half ounce of mace, and two teaspoonfuls of cloves. Do not use ground spices.
Boil for fifteen minutes.
When cold, strain, and to each quart of juice add 3/4 cup of whiskey.
Bottle and seal.

notes: Use whole spices, not ground

recipes.title: Blueberry Cobbler
recipes.description: Mountain blueberry cobbler with sweet biscuit topping.

instructions.text: Cook berries for fifteen minutes over medium heat with one cup sugar.
For dough, use two cups flour and two tablespoons each of sugar and shortening with a pinch of salt and two teaspoons baking powder. Add enough milk to mix.
Drop dough by spoonfuls onto hot berries and bake until golden.

recipes.title: Blueberry Crisp
recipes.description: A simple blueberry crisp with oat topping.

instructions.text: Put berries in a greased baking dish and sprinkle with 1/3 cup sugar.
For topping, cream butter and brown sugar.
Blend in flour and oats with a fork.
Spread over berries and bake.

recipes.title: Blueberry Dessert Rolls
recipes.description: Rolled biscuit dough filled with blueberries, baked upside down.

instructions.text: Cook berries and drain thoroughly.
Make dough from biscuit mix and milk.
Roll out dough, brush with butter, and sprinkle with sugar and cinnamon.
Cover with blueberries.
Roll up like a jelly roll. Place seam side down in a greased baking dish.
Bake in a hot oven (425°) about thirty minutes.

recipes.title: Sumac Lemonade
recipes.description: A refreshing pink lemonade-like drink made from sumac berries. Said to relieve fatigue and reduce fever.

instructions.text: Crush sumac berries.
Cover with boiling water.
Steep until well colored.
Strain through a cloth.
Sweeten with sugar or honey and serve cold.

notes: Prepare and serve at once - will not keep
Use red sumac (staghorn or smooth), NOT poison sumac which has white berries

flags: Use only red sumac, never white-berried poison sumac

recipes.title: Sumac and Elderberry Jelly
recipes.description: A unique jelly combining tart sumac with sweet elderberries.

instructions.text: Boil one pint sumac berries in three pints water.
Add one pint elderberries.
Strain through cloth.
Add one cup sugar for each cup juice and cook into jelly.

recipes.title: Gooseberry Pie
recipes.description: A classic gooseberry pie with lattice top.

instructions.text: Mix two cups berries with 3/4 cup sugar and cook until soft and clear.
Pour into a pie shell.
Lay strips of pie dough crosswise on the berries.
Bake at about 450° until the crust is golden.

notes: Wild gooseberries are prickly but very sweet inside

recipes.title: Elderberry Jelly
recipes.description: Classic elderberry jelly.

instructions.text: Cook elderberries with a small amount of water until thoroughly cooked.
Strain, and to one pint juice, add one pound sugar.
Cook until it jellies.

recipes.title: Spiced Elderberries
recipes.description: Spiced preserved elderberries.

instructions.text: Wash elderberries and pack in self-sealing jars with a half teaspoon each of cloves and allspice.
Cover with vinegar.
Boil one cup of sugar and pour over the berries.
Seal while hot.

recipes.title: Wild Strawberry Jam
recipes.description: Jam from tiny wild strawberries. As they say, 'If it is four o'clock by the time you get your clothes on, it will be light enough to pick strawberries.'

instructions.text: Put a quart of berries in a pot, add a cup of sugar, and bring to a boil, stirring gently.
Boil three minutes, add another cup of sugar and boil three more minutes.
Add a final cup of sugar, skim off foam and put in jars and seal.

notes: Wild strawberries are rich in iron and vitamin C

recipes.title: Wild Strawberry Preserves
recipes.description: Old-fashioned strawberry preserves that rest overnight.

instructions.text: To a quart of strawberries, add one cup of sugar and three tablespoons water.
Boil slowly fifteen minutes. Let stand overnight.
Next morning, bring to boiling point and pour in jars while hot.

recipes.title: Strawberry Leather
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian fruit leather from Foxfire 2
recipes.description: Sun-dried strawberry leather, rolled up like a jelly cake.

instructions.text: Mash ripe berries to pulp.
Spread on platters.
When dry, dust with sugar and roll up like a jelly cake into pieces.
Pack into clean jars.

notes: A traditional method of preserving fruit before glass jars were available

recipes.title: Wild Strawberry Pie
recipes.description: Fresh strawberry pie with syrup topping.

instructions.text: Sift flour, mix with lard, salt, cold water, and vinegar. Mix well and roll out dough.
Put in greased pie pan. Bake fifteen minutes.
Make filling of one cup crushed strawberries, one-half cup sugar, two tablespoons cornstarch, and one cup water. Cook into a syrup.
Fill pie crust with fresh strawberries, pour syrup over top and serve.

recipes.title: Strawberry Mallow
recipes.description: A chilled strawberry and marshmallow dessert.

instructions.text: Mix together strawberries, sugar, salt, marshmallows, and cream.
Chill.
Top with whole berries.

recipes.title: Mixed Wild Greens
recipes.description: A 'mess' of mixed wild greens with salt pork and vinegar.

instructions.text: Get together a mess of poke, dandelion, lamb's quarters, violet leaves, and sour dock.
Mix together and cook.
Drain and season with bits of fried salt pork, and a little vinegar.

notes: Any mild-flavored green can be combined with sharper mustards and cresses

recipes.title: Mixed Wild Green Salad
recipes.description: A raw salad of wild spring greens with garlic dressing.

instructions.text: Take equal parts of dandelion, shepherd's purse, peppergrass, curly dock, poke shoots (must be cooked first), and sorrel. Chop fine.
Add wild onion to taste.
Make a dressing of oil and vinegar, and flavor with garlic, mustard, salt, and pepper.
Serve on a bed of wild dock or lettuce leaves.

notes: Poke shoots MUST be cooked before adding to raw salad

recipes.title: Canned Wild Greens
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian canning method from Foxfire 2
recipes.description: How to can wild greens for winter use.

instructions.text: Mix mustard and wild turnip greens, or buff sallet and mustard mixed, or with creases.
Fix and precook until tender.
Put in jars, add water, seal.
Cook thirty minutes in pressure cooker.

notes: Most wild sallets can be canned this way

recipes.title: Wilted Greens with Hot Bacon Dressing
recipes.description: Wild greens wilted with hot bacon and vinegar dressing.

instructions.text: Fry bacon until crisp.
Add vinegar and salt to the hot bacon grease.
Pour over the greens and toss.

recipes.title: Persimmon Bread
recipes.description: Cornmeal bread with ripe persimmons.

instructions.text: Mix everything together.
Add water if mixture is not thin enough.
Bake like cornbread.

notes: To be good, a raw persimmon must be soft and squishy to the touch

recipes.title: Persimmon Beer
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian fermented drink from Foxfire 3
recipes.description: A potent fermented drink made from persimmons and honey locust pods.

instructions.text: Gather persimmons and a good number of honey locust seed pods. Wash them both well.
Place them in a large crock in layers until the crock is full.
Pour enough boiling water in to cover them.
Cover the churn and let it sit at least a week.
Pour off or dip out the beer as desired.
When drained, the churn may be filled with boiling water again to make a second batch.

notes: The beer is supposed to be very potent

recipes.title: Persimmon Pudding
recipes.description: A rich baked persimmon pudding.

instructions.text: Strain persimmons through a colander.
Stir all ingredients together.
Put in greased pan.
Bake one hour at low heat.

notes: Persimmons are very high in food energy

recipes.title: Persimmon Pie
recipes.description: A spiced persimmon custard pie with meringue topping.

instructions.text: Peel and crush persimmons until smooth.
Add sugar and beat. Add three egg yolks and one egg white.
Add milk, nutmeg, and salt. Beat until smooth.
Pour into nine-inch pie shell and bake until done.
Make meringue by beating whites of remaining eggs until stiff. Add four tablespoons sugar.
Put on top of pie and brown in moderate oven.

recipes.title: Persimmon-Nut Bread
recipes.description: A sweet quick bread with persimmons and hickory nuts or black walnuts.

instructions.text: Cream shortening, add sugar and eggs; beat well.
Sift dry ingredients, add to creamed mixture alternately with persimmons and nuts.
Pour in greased loaf pan and bake at 350° for one hour.

recipes.title: Candied Persimmons
recipes.description: Persimmons preserved with sugar until candied.

instructions.text: Pack persimmons in jars, alternating with layers of sugar.
Put on lids and store in a cool place until they become candied.

recipes.title: Persimmon Butter
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian fruit butter from Foxfire 3
recipes.description: A spiced persimmon spread like apple butter.

instructions.text: Cook and strain persimmons.
Add 1/2 teaspoon soda to each cup pulp.
Sweeten and flavor with spices or orange rind.
Cook thoroughly and bottle.

recipes.title: Pawpaw Pie
recipes.description: A custard pie made from pawpaws, which taste 'somewheres between a banana and a persimmon.'

instructions.text: Place sugar, milk, egg, salt, and pawpaws in a stew pan and stir together.
Cook until thickened.
Pour in an unbaked pie shell and bake until done.

notes: Pawpaws ripen in late autumn and taste like a cross between banana and persimmon

recipes.title: Pawpaw Bread
recipes.description: Nut bread with pawpaw pulp that gives it a lovely rose-red color.

instructions.text: Add pawpaw pulp to your favorite nut bread recipe.
Bake as directed. It gives bread a lovely rose-red color.

recipes.title: Wild Plum Catsup
recipes.description: A spiced plum catsup for meats.

instructions.text: Boil plums with one teaspoon soda. Bring to a rolling boil.
Strain through a colander.
Simmer with sugar, vinegar, and spices until thick as catsup.

notes: Chickasaw plums have the best-tasting fruit

recipes.title: Wild Plum Cobbler
recipes.description: A layered plum cobbler with strips of biscuit dough.

instructions.text: Cook and pit one quart plums.
Roll biscuit dough thin and cut in strips.
Grease a pan well and add a layer of plums and strips of dough, topping with sugar and dabs of butter.
Repeat until pan is almost full.
Bake in medium oven.

recipes.title: Wild Plum Pudding
recipes.description: A baked plum pudding with cake-like topping.

instructions.text: Put pitted, cooked, sweetened plums two inches deep in bottom of a baking dish.
Beat one cup sugar, four tablespoons butter, and one egg to a cream.
Add one scant cup of milk, two cups all-purpose flour, and two teaspoons baking powder.
Mix well, and pour over plums.
Bake one hour at 350°.

recipes.title: Wild Plum Conserve
recipes.description: A rich conserve with plums, oranges, and raisins.

instructions.text: Wash and pick over plums. Cover with boiling water, and add 1/2 teaspoon soda.
Bring to rolling boil. Pour off the soda water, rinse plums, and strain through a colander.
Slice oranges in thin slices, rind and all, removing seeds, and grind the raisins.
Combine fruit and sugar, adding enough water to keep them from sticking.
Simmer until thick and clear.

recipes.title: Wild Plum Jelly
recipes.description: Classic wild plum jelly.

instructions.text: Cover 1/2 gallon half-ripe plums with water in a porcelain kettle.
Boil ten minutes.
Pour off the juice and strain through flannel.
Add one pound sugar to each pint juice.
Boil until it will harden when cold (about twenty to thirty minutes).

notes: Use half-ripe plums for best jelling

recipes.title: Sugared Nut Meats
recipes.description: Spiced candied nuts with rum flavoring.

instructions.text: Cream oil, sugar, flavoring and spices.
Spread nuts on cookie sheet, heat in moderate oven ten minutes.
Turn hot nuts into the cream mixture and stir.
Separate and spread on a cookie sheet to cool.

notes: Can use walnuts, hickory nuts, or hazelnuts

recipes.title: Nut Brittle Squares
recipes.description: Caramelized sugar poured over nuts for a simple brittle.

instructions.text: Butter the outside bottom of an eight-inch-square pan.
Spread evenly with one cup finely chopped nuts.
Set pan, nut side up, on a tray.
Put one cup sugar in skillet and heat, stirring until golden brown and syrupy.
Pour over nuts at once.
When slightly cooled, remove in one piece to a board and cut into two-inch squares.

notes: Works with walnuts, hickory nuts, or hazelnuts

recipes.title: Chestnut Croquettes
recipes.description: Sweet fried chestnut balls.

instructions.text: Mix one cup mashed, boiled chestnuts with 1/4 teaspoon vanilla, two beaten egg yolks, two tablespoons cream, one teaspoon sugar.
Shape in balls, roll in crumbs.
Fry in deep fat.

notes: American chestnuts are now rare due to blight but still occasionally found

recipes.title: Acorn Coffee
recipes.description: A coffee substitute made from roasted acorns. 'Real good, just as good as bought coffee.'

instructions.text: Parch acorns until thoroughly dry but not burned.
Grind into powder.
Brew like coffee. It makes a red coffee.

notes: White oak acorns are sweetest; also use chestnut oak or yellow chestnut oak

recipes.title: Acorn Indian Pudding
recipes.description: A cornmeal-style pudding made with acorn meal and sorghum.

instructions.text: Put three cups water on to boil.
Mix acorn meal with remaining cup of water, stir until smooth.
Add to boiling water, stir until thickened.
Add sorghum syrup to taste.
Cover and cook fifteen minutes at low heat.

notes: Acorn meal was once a staple of pioneer diet when times were rough

recipes.title: Elderflower Fritters
recipes.description: Battered and fried elderflower clusters.

instructions.text: Dip elderflower clusters in fritter batter.
Fry in fat.
Dust with powdered sugar and serve.

recipes.title: Elderberry-Apple-Orange Jam
recipes.description: A complex jam combining elderberries with apples and citrus.

instructions.text: Cook apples until mushy.
Add the berries, oranges, and lemon chopped fine.
Add sugar and cook until thick.

recipes.title: Stuffed Grape Leaves
recipes.description: Grape leaves stuffed with meat and rice.

instructions.text: Mix ground meat with cooked rice, onion, and seasonings.
Place filling on grape leaves and roll up.
Steam or bake until done.

recipes.title: Spiced Grapes
recipes.description: Pickled spiced grapes.

instructions.text: Stem and wash five pounds grapes.
Boil one and one-half pints of good apple vinegar with sugar and one stick cinnamon and half teaspoon allspice.
Add grapes and boil until thick.
Bottle and seal while hot.

recipes.title: Mayapple Marmalade
recipes.description: A marmalade from ripe mayapple fruits with their strawberry-like flavor.

instructions.text: Gather ripe fruits and simmer until soft.
Strain through a colander.
Boil the pulp with sugar to taste.

notes: CAUTION: Only the ripe fruit is edible - all other parts of the plant are poisonous
Green mayapples can cause stomach ache

flags: Only ripe fruit is safe - rest of plant is poisonous

recipes.title: Groundcherry Preserves
recipes.description: Preserves made from groundcherries (husk tomatoes).

instructions.text: Remove husks from groundcherries and wash.
Combine with sugar, water, and lemon juice.
Cook slowly until thick.
Pour into jars and seal.

notes: Also called cape gooseberry or husk tomato

recipes.title: Black Walnut Pudding
recipes.description: A rich pudding with black walnuts.

instructions.text: Beat egg yolks with sugar until light.
Add milk and flour, cook until thickened.
Add vanilla and walnuts.
Fold in stiffly beaten egg whites.
Pour into baking dish and bake until set.

recipes.title: Pickled Walnuts
recipes.description: Green walnuts pickled in spiced vinegar.

instructions.text: Gather green walnuts before the shell hardens (test with a needle).
Soak in brine for nine days, changing brine every three days.
Drain and spread on trays in sun until they turn black.
Pack in jars.
Boil vinegar with spices and pour over walnuts.
Seal and store.

notes: Must use young green walnuts before shell hardens

recipes.title: Aunt Arie's Leather Breeches Beans
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian preserved beans from Foxfire 2
recipes.description: Dried green beans strung and hung from the rafters, then rehydrated and cooked with pork.

instructions.text: Take good, full green beans and string them on spool thread, breaking off the ends. Hang from rafters in warm, dark attic (not in sun or open air).
To cook: take down as many strings as needed and soak overnight.
In the morning, parboil for an hour with a little soda added (not over a teaspoon or they'll turn yellow).
Take them out, wash and rinse them.
Put in a pot with clear water and several large chunks of fat pork.
Cook for two or three hours more until soft and done.

notes: If beans are 'nothin' but slabs, they ain't fit t'eat' - use good, full beans

recipes.title: Ada Kelly's Fermented Cornbread
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian fermented cornbread from Foxfire 2
recipes.description: An old-fashioned cornbread made with fermented cornmeal mush.

instructions.text: Cook one quart of corn meal mush until thoroughly done. Salt to taste.
Remove from heat and add cold water until you can bear your finger in it.
Add 3/4 cup sugar, 3/4 cup lard, and meal enough to make stiff as cornbread.
Set aside until it ferments (overnight).
Add meal to make medium batter.
Bake in well-greased pan in slow oven. Remove from pan when cold.

recipes.title: Icicle Pickles
recipes.description: Sweet, crisp cucumber pickles that take about two weeks to make.

instructions.text: Split cucumbers lengthwise, no matter how small. Add salt to boiling water and pour over cucumbers. Let stand one week.
Drain, cover with boiling water again and let stand twenty-four hours.
Drain, dissolve alum in boiling water and pour over pickles. Let stand twenty-four hours.
Drain. Boil vinegar, sugar, and all spices together and pour over pickles.
Do this for four mornings - pouring off liquid, reboiling it, and pouring back over pickles boiling hot.
Seal in cans.

notes: Will also keep in an open jar but most people seal them for winter

recipes.title: Lime Pickles
recipes.description: Crisp pickles made with builder's lime for extra crunch.

instructions.text: Let tomatoes or cucumbers soak with lime and water for twenty-four hours.
Then let pickles soak in clear water for four hours, changing water every hour.
Make syrup of vinegar, sugar, and pickling spice and bring to a boil.
Add cucumbers and let stand overnight.
Boil for one hour, pack in glass jars, and seal.

recipes.title: Spiced Grapes Relish
recipes.description: A spiced grape relish used with meat and bread.

instructions.text: Wash, stem, and pulp grapes.
Put pulp with seeds over fire and cook until seeds come free.
Add skins and pulp together, and also add sugar, vinegar, and spices.
Cook until thick and can.

recipes.title: Pickled Green Tomatoes
recipes.description: Hot and sweet pickled green tomatoes.

instructions.text: Wash and quarter green tomatoes. Pack raw into pint jars.
Add to each jar two-three small whole pods of hot pepper and one quartered pod of bell pepper.
Make brine of two parts vinegar, one part water, one part sugar; heat until sugar melts.
Pour into packed jars leaving half-inch at top.
Put on lids and rings and process fifteen minutes in water bath.

recipes.title: Pickled Peaches or Apples
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian pickled fruit from Foxfire 2
recipes.description: Spiced pickled peaches or apples.

instructions.text: Peel apples or peaches, quarter, and put in a pot.
Make enough brine of two parts vinegar, two parts sugar, and one part water to cover fruit.
Add ground cinnamon, nutmeg, and allspice to taste, and cook until tender.
When done, lift fruit out and pack into jars.
Keep brine simmering and pour into jars over fruit leaving one-half inch at top.
Seal immediately.

recipes.title: Aunt Arie's Egg Custard
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian custard pie from Foxfire 2
recipes.description: A simple egg custard pie baked on a wood stove.

instructions.text: Line a small pie pan with plain biscuit dough rolled thin.
In a separate bowl, mix up one egg (beaten well), one cup of sweet milk, a handful of flour, a teaspoon of nutmeg, half a teacup of sugar.
Mix it all up well, pour into the crust.
Using just a little wood so the fire won't be too hot, bake slowly until it 'sets.'
It will 'blubber up' - or bubble, and then the bubbles will settle. At this point it is ready to eat.

notes: Originally cooked on a wood stove

recipes.title: Sweet Potato Pudding
recipes.description: A baked sweet potato pudding with raisins and coconut.

instructions.text: Mix together all ingredients.
Bake in a casserole dish in a moderate oven for about half-hour, or until firm.
Serve hot or cold.

recipes.title: Irish Potato Dumplings
recipes.description: Biscuit dumplings cooked in creamy potato broth.

instructions.text: Put quartered potatoes in pot, cover with water, add salt, pepper, butter, and milk.
Boil until potatoes are tender.
Roll biscuit dough out one-quarter-inch thick, cut in two-inch squares.
Drop into the rapidly boiling water the potatoes are in.
Cook dumplings about one minute, take the pot off the heat, and serve.

recipes.title: Pepper Sauce (Hot Pepper Relish)
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian hot pepper sauce from Foxfire 2
recipes.description: A hot pepper and onion relish.

instructions.text: Chop onions and peppers up fine.
Pour boiling water over them and let stand for five minutes, then drain.
Put back in kettle and pour on more boiling water, let boil two minutes, drain.
Put back in kettle again.
Add vinegar, sugar, and salt and boil for fifteen minutes.
Can while hot.

recipes.title: Mint with New Peas
recipes.description: Fresh mint cooked with young peas.

instructions.text: Tear young mint leaves in pieces.
Cook with very young peas.

notes: Use spearmint or peppermint

recipes.title: Mint Syrup
recipes.description: A sweet mint syrup for fresh fruit or puddings.

instructions.text: Stir together sugar, water, and mint leaves.
Simmer until sugar is completely dissolved.
Cover and let stand one hour.
Strain and use over fresh fruit or puddings.

recipes.title: Mint Jelly
recipes.description: Fresh mint jelly, traditionally served with lamb.

instructions.text: Do not boil leaves, but pour boiling water over them and let steep.
Strain.
Add sugar and pectin.
Cook until it jells.

recipes.title: Mint Vinegar
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian flavored vinegar from Foxfire 3
recipes.description: Mint-infused vinegar that ripens over several weeks.

instructions.text: Let mint stand covered by sugar for five minutes.
Bring vinegar to a boil.
Add mint and sugar to vinegar and boil three minutes.
Strain through cheesecloth and bottle.
Let stand several weeks to ripen.

recipes.title: Mint Sauce
recipes.description: Classic mint sauce for lamb.

instructions.text: Chop mint very fine.
Dissolve sugar in vinegar.
Add mint and let stand one hour.
Strain and serve.

recipes.title: Mint Frosting
recipes.description: A fresh mint frosting for cakes.

instructions.text: Chop young mint leaves fine.
Mix with powdered sugar, soft butter, and drops of cream.

recipes.title: Fig Preserves
recipes.description: Simple fig preserves.

instructions.text: Put figs in a pan, and add sugar until it covers the figs.
Let stand overnight.
In the morning, cook until thick and clear.
Put in jars and seal.

notes: Figs should be picked in early morning

recipes.title: Fig Pudding
recipes.description: A rice pudding with figs and nuts.

instructions.text: Mix rice, milk, beaten egg, figs, nuts, and spices.
Add vanilla and melted butter.
Pour into greased baking dish and bake.

recipes.title: Honey Figs
recipes.description: Fresh figs drizzled with honey.

instructions.text: Peel figs and cut in half.
Arrange in serving dish.
Pour a thin honey over them.

recipes.title: Crabapple Jelly
recipes.description: Classic crabapple jelly, can add mint leaves if desired.

instructions.text: Simmer crabapples twenty minutes. Mash in pan.
Strain. Add one cup sugar to one cup juice.
Add mint leaves if desired.
Put in jars, and set in a dark place to thicken.

notes: Crabapples were often added to blackberries or blueberries to help jelly set

recipes.title: Crabapple Butter
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian fruit butter from Foxfire 3
recipes.description: A spiced crabapple butter.

instructions.text: Cook crabapples with peelings and run through a food mill.
Boil slowly until thick.
Add sugar and spices and cook until thick.
Pour into jars and seal.

recipes.title: Sweet Pickled Crabapples
recipes.description: Spiced pickled crabapples.

instructions.text: Wash crabapples. Cut out blossom ends, but leave stems intact.
Combine sugar, spices, vinegar, and water in large saucepan and heat until sugar dissolves.
Add crabapples and simmer gently until tender.
Pack in jars, pour syrup over, and seal.

recipes.title: Yarrow Tea
recipes.description: A bracing, warming tea from yarrow leaves.

instructions.text: Place dry or green yarrow leaves in a cup.
Pour hot water over them.
Steep only until color shows.
Drink without sweetening.

notes: Good and warming in cold weather

recipes.title: Fried Yarrow
recipes.description: Yarrow leaves fried in butter and served with orange juice.

instructions.text: Fry yarrow in butter until brown.
Serve hot, sprinkled with sugar and the juice of an orange.

recipes.title: Chamomile Tea
recipes.description: A pleasant-tasting tea from chamomile flower heads.

ingredients.prep_note: gathered at noon when sun is shining

instructions.text: Gather flower heads at noon when the sun is shining (dried blooms will retain better flavor).
Pour hot water over flower heads.
Steep and strain.

recipes.title: Pennyroyal Tea
recipes.description: The best-tasting of the wild mint teas, helpful for coughs and colds.

instructions.text: Use fresh or dried leaves. Do not boil.
Merely pour hot water over the leaves and let stand for a few minutes.
Flavor with syrup or honey.

notes: Also called penny-rile or squaw-mint

recipes.title: Blue-Mountain Tea
recipes.description: A delicious licorice-flavored tea from a special goldenrod that grows in the Blue Ridge Mountains.

instructions.text: Steep green or dry leaves in hot water until the tea is a pale golden color.
Add sugar, honey, or lemon if desired.
Can be served hot or cold.

notes: Has a distinctive licorice taste and odor - impossible to mistake for any other plant

recipes.title: Possum Haw Jelly
recipes.description: Jelly from possum haw berries, often combined with crabapples.

instructions.text: Boil berries until soft.
Strain through cloth.
Add sugar to taste.
Boil again until thickened.
Combine with crabapples if desired.

notes: Haw berries are extremely seedy

recipes.title: Black Haw Sauce
recipes.description: A honey-sweetened sauce from black haw berries.

instructions.text: Wash berries well.
Cook with honey and lemon juice until soft.
Strain and serve.

recipes.title: Red Haw (Hawthorn) Relish
recipes.description: A spiced relish from hawthorn fruits.

instructions.text: Crush three pounds fruit (not too ripe).
Add four cups water and cook until soft.
Strain through cloth.
Add sugar, vinegar, and spices.
Boil until thick. Bottle and seal.

recipes.title: Haw Marmalade
recipes.description: A marmalade from hawthorn fruits.

instructions.text: Cook haws in very little water.
Press through a colander to remove seeds.
Add sugar to taste.
Cook until thick and bottle.

recipes.title: Mrs. Reese's Pressed Cheese
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian cheese-making from Foxfire Book 4
recipes.description: A traditional pressed cheese that forms a dry crust and keeps for a month or more. Uses rennet tablets to curdle the milk.

instructions.text: Pour all the milk into a large pan and heat on a wood stove (for slower, steadier heat) until a little past lukewarm.
Remove from heat and add the dissolved rennet tablet and color tablet.
Let sit for 15-30 minutes until the milk stiffens and becomes jelly-like.
Cut the curd with a knife or spatula into tiny squares, also running the spatula under the surface as if cutting it into layers.
Let sit briefly, then gently work the mixture until broken into pieces the size of grains of corn.
Return pan to stove and heat slowly, stirring constantly, until almost as hot as the touch can stand but not boiling.
Remove from heat and let sit 15-30 minutes to cool.
Strain contents through cheesecloth in a colander. Let drip naturally, do not squeeze.
Return curds to pan, add the salt, and massage it in well.
Put curds into a homemade press lined with cheesecloth. Add weight in stages and leave overnight (12 hours).
Remove from press and dry in open air for one week, turning twice daily. The cheese forms a dry crust on the outside.

notes: Before rennet tablets were available, a piece of dried cow stomach lining (about thumbnail size) was used to curdle the milk.
A wood stove is preferred for its slower, steadier heat.
The cheese keeps for a month or more without refrigeration.

recipes.title: Mrs. Thelma Earp's Quick Fried Cheese
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian cheese-making from Foxfire Book 4
recipes.description: A quick cheese that can be eaten right away, made by frying curds in butter. Forms a cake as it cools.

ingredients.prep_note: raw, barnyard eggs preferred for color

instructions.text: Allow cream to rise on whole milk, skim it off and make butter.
Add 2-3 tablespoons buttermilk per gallon of skimmed milk and let sit out for two days to sour.
Refrigerate the clabbered milk until ready to use.
Pour clabbered milk into a pan and heat until a little hotter than lukewarm (pretty hot but not boiling, won't burn hands).
Pour into a strainer made with cotton cloth pinned over a bucket. Squeeze the whey through, leaving curds.
Put curds in a bowl, add salt and raw egg. Mix with hands.
Melt butter in a large iron frying pan. Prefer wood stove for even, slow heat.
Add curds and keep turning in the pan over medium heat until all curds melt and run together into a cake.
Put out into a dish to cool. It automatically forms a cake as it cools.

notes: Can be eaten right away or kept several days.
Do not refrigerate - it should dry out somewhat.
After a short while it gets hard enough to cut into slices.
Keeps about a week.
Feed the whey to the hogs.

recipes.title: Appalachian Cottage Cheese
recipes.attribution: Mrs. Harriet Echols and Mrs. Nora Garland, via Foxfire 4
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian cottage cheese from Foxfire Book 4
recipes.description: Simple cottage cheese made by clabbering raw milk, then heating and draining the curds.

instructions.text: Pour raw milk into an enamel or metal pan.
Let sit on back of wood stove (winter) or kitchen table (warm weather) to sour slowly. Takes 1-2 days depending on temperature.
After milk clabbers, lift off the cream and refrigerate (can be used as sour cream or mixed back in later).
Heat the skimmed clabbered milk over low fire until it curdles.
Remove from heat and pour into a colander or cheesecloth to drain. Takes a couple of hours. Can hang in a clean flour sack overnight.
Work the cheese by squeezing with hands or spoon to remove remaining water. Don't work too vigorously or get curds too fine.
Sprinkle in salt to taste. For creamier cheese, mix in some of the reserved sour cream.
Package in small containers and refrigerate. Keeps several weeks.

notes: Do not heat the milk before it clabbers.
Mrs. Garland put the curdled milk in a clean flour sack and let it drain outside overnight.

recipes.title: Pearl's Sassafras Jelly
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian sassafras jelly recipe from Foxfire Book 4
recipes.description: A unique jelly made from sassafras tea, capturing the distinctive flavor of this Appalachian root.

ingredients.prep_note: made by boiling 4 roots in 1 gallon water for 15-20 minutes

instructions.text: Make sassafras tea: Boil 4 average-sized sassafras roots in 1 gallon of water for 15-20 minutes. The longer boiled, the stronger the tea. Strain.
Mix one package of Sure-Jell with 8 cups of sassafras tea in a large saucepan.
Bring quickly to a hard boil, stirring occasionally.
Add 8 cups sugar and bring to a full rolling boil.
Boil hard one minute, stirring constantly.
Skim off foam with a metal spoon.
Pour at once into jelly jars and seal with paraffin.

notes: Pearl also makes sassafras tea, serving it hot or iced, sweetened with sugar or honey.
Sassafras tea can be made stronger or weaker by adjusting boiling time.

recipes.title: Mrs. Parker's Bleached Apple Pie
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian bleached apple pie from Foxfire Book 4
recipes.description: A pie made with sulfur-bleached apples that taste like fresh apples even months after preserving.

instructions.text: Preheat oven to 350°F (175°C).
Place several cups of bleached apple pieces in an uncooked pie crust.
Add butter, sugar, and cinnamon to taste.
Cover with pastry strips or a second crust if preferred.
Bake for 30-35 minutes or until crust is golden brown.

notes: Bleached apples are preserved using sulfur smoke in a special box.
Use as little water as possible when cooking bleached apples - water brings back the sulfur taste.
The sulfur taste is not noticeable when apples are eaten dry.

recipes.title: Blanche Harkins' Fried Apple Pies
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian fried apple pies from Foxfire Book 4
recipes.description: Traditional half-moon shaped pies filled with spiced dried apples, fried until golden. Yellow apples make tastier pies.

instructions.text: To dry apples: Peel and core apples, cut into thin slices. Soak in salt water, drain, lay on flat board or pan on white cloth. Dry outside in sunshine for several days until shrunk to half size. Store in sacks in dry place.
To prepare filling: Add small amount of water to dried apples and cook until tender. Mash with a fork. Add sugar and cinnamon or allspice to taste.
Make pie crust: Mix 4 cups self-rising flour with 1/2 cup Crisco and 1 cup water. Work like regular pie crust.
Divide dough into fist-sized balls (one per pie).
Roll each ball into a very thin circle.
Place cooked apples on one half of the circle.
Fold crust over apples and press edges together with fingers or fork.
Make tiny holes or slits in top with fork or knife to let air out.
Put enough Crisco in large iron frying pan to almost cover the pies. Fry until golden.
Alternatively, brush with melted butter and bake for crisp crust.

notes: Yellow apples make tastier pies than red.
The holes in the crust prevent edges from turning up during cooking.
Can be baked instead of fried - brush with melted butter before baking.

recipes.title: Mrs. Brown's Apple Cider
recipes.attribution: Mrs. Harry Brown of Betty's Creek Community, via Foxfire 4
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian apple cider from Foxfire Book 4
recipes.description: Old-fashioned apple cider made with a traditional cider press, using a mix of sour and sweet apples.

instructions.text: Wash apples thoroughly.
Use a proportion of half sour and half sweet apples. Adjust ratio for sweeter or more tart cider.
Place whole apples into the wooden hopper of the cider mill.
Turn the mill crank to crush apples. Pulp drops into a slatted, bottomless tub.
When tub is full, move it under the screw press.
Fit wooden disc into top of tub and turn the screw to press disc down onto apple pulp, squeezing out all juice.
Strain cider through cheesecloth into pans or pitchers.
Serve fresh, or preserve by canning or freezing.

notes: Any type of apples can be used.
For sweeter cider, add more sweet apples; for more tart, add more sour apples.
Cider can be preserved by canning or freezing.
Mrs. Brown prefers freezing to canning.

recipes.title: Switchell (Honey-Vinegar Drink)
recipes.source_note: Traditional drink for hot summer haymaking days from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A nourishing drink made from honey and cider vinegar, traditionally consumed during haymaking days in summer.

instructions.text: Mix half cup honey and half cup cider vinegar together.
Keep in a jar.
To serve, add four teaspoons of the mixture to a dipper of water for a nourishing drink.

notes: A traditional drink for hot summer haymaking days.

recipes.title: Violet Jelly
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food recipe from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A delicate jelly made from wild violet flowers.

instructions.text: Cook violet flowers with boiling water.
Strain the liquid.
Add sugar, pectin, and juice of half a lemon.
Simmer until it jells.
Pour into jars and seal.

notes: Violet flowers give this jelly a beautiful color and delicate flavor.

recipes.title: Sugared Violets
recipes.description: Crystallized violet blossoms for decoration or eating.

instructions.text: Cook two cups sugar, half cup water, and a dash of cream of tartar.
Stir until sugar grains (crystallizes).
Dip fresh violet blossoms (free from stems) into the sugar mixture.
Place on platter to dry.

notes: Beautiful for decorating cakes or eating as confections.

recipes.title: Violet Syrup
recipes.source_note: Traditional cold remedy from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: A medicinal syrup made from violet blossoms, good for colds or coughs.

instructions.text: Cover violet blossoms with water.
Let stand two days.
Strain the liquid.
Cook with honey and juice of lemon.
Stir well and bring to a boil.
Put in jars and seal.

notes: Good for colds or coughs.

recipes.title: Fried Milkweed
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food recipe from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Young milkweed shoots fried with eggs and cheese.

instructions.text: Cut young milkweed shoots in small pieces.
Boil fifteen minutes in salted water.
Drain well.
Fry in small amount of fat.
Add eggs, salt and pepper, and cheese if desired.

notes: Only use very young shoots before leaves unfold. Do not gather milkweed after July.

recipes.title: Milkweed Soup
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food recipe from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Hearty soup made from milkweed shoots or young pods.

instructions.text: For shoots: Gather young shoots while young and tender (not after July). Wash, cook, and drain.
Add more water, rice, bacon drippings, salt, pepper, and wild onions.
Cook over a slow fire until done.
For pods: Boil a hambone in water.
Add young milkweed pods cut in small pieces, wild onions or ramps, and a handful of rice.
Cook slowly. Add salt and pepper before serving.

notes: Two methods: one using shoots, one using young pods. Only gather milkweed before July.

recipes.title: Milkweed Greens
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food recipe from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Simple preparation of young milkweed stalks as a green vegetable.

instructions.text: Cook one pound very young milkweed stalks in water with salt and butter, covered, for ten minutes.
Drain.
Add more butter and chopped wild onions.

notes: In Tennessee and Kentucky, milkweed is considered a tonic, 'good for what ails you.'

recipes.title: Chicory with Sauce
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food recipe from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Chicory greens served with a tangy mustard sauce.

instructions.text: Cook chicory greens and drain well.
Make sauce: combine sugar, salt, egg yolks, scalded milk, vinegar, and mustard.
Blend until thick in a double boiler.
Serve sauce over the drained chicory.

notes: The tangy sauce complements the slightly bitter chicory greens.

recipes.title: Panned Chicory
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food recipe from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Quick pan-steamed chicory greens in cream sauce.

instructions.text: Melt two tablespoons fat in pan.
Add chopped chicory greens.
Cover and steam for fifteen minutes.
Add one tablespoon flour, a small amount of cream, salt and pepper.
Let simmer five minutes more.

notes: A quick and creamy way to prepare wild chicory.

recipes.title: Chicory Coffee
recipes.source_note: Traditional coffee substitute from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Roasted chicory root used as a coffee substitute or additive.

instructions.text: Wash and peel chicory roots.
Grind the roots.
Roast in oven until dark brown.
Add to regular coffee, or use instead of coffee.

notes: Popular during times when coffee was scarce or expensive.

recipes.title: Dandelion Bud Omelet
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food recipe from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Fluffy omelet made with dandelion buds fried in butter.

instructions.text: Gather one cup dandelion buds before flower color shows.
Fry buds in a dab of butter until they pop.
Add four eggs, salt and pepper.
Cook as an omelet.
Top with raw dandelion leaves, finely cut, before serving.

notes: Gather buds before they show any yellow color for best flavor.

recipes.title: Dandelion Wine
recipes.source_note: Traditional wine recipe from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Classic homemade wine made from dandelion flowers.

instructions.text: Pour one gallon boiling water over one gallon dandelion flowers.
Let stand until blossoms rise (24-48 hours).
Strain into a stone jar.
Add juices of four lemons and four oranges, four pounds of sugar, and one yeast cake.
Stir four or five times a day until it stops fermenting.
Keep well covered.
In two weeks, strain, bottle and cork tightly.

notes: A traditional spring wine. Use only the flower petals, not the green parts.

recipes.title: Dandelion Coffee
recipes.source_note: Traditional coffee substitute from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Roasted dandelion root used as a coffee substitute.

instructions.text: Gather dandelion roots.
Peel the roots.
Roast until dark brown.
Grind.
Use as substitute for real coffee.

notes: A caffeine-free coffee alternative with a slightly bitter, nutty flavor.

recipes.title: Green Drink Tonic
recipes.description: A healthful tonic drink made from chickweed and dandelion.

instructions.text: Cook chickweed and dandelion separately.
Put each through a sieve.
Add cider vinegar to the combined purees.
Drink as a tonic.

notes: A spring tonic to cleanse the system after winter.

recipes.title: Wild Lettuce Salad
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food recipe from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Fresh salad made with wild lettuce and hot bacon dressing.

instructions.text: Cut up wild lettuce greens and wash.
Cut green onions in it.
Fry bacon until crisp and crumbly.
Add brown sugar and vinegar to the hot bacon grease.
Pour hot dressing over the chopped wild lettuce leaves.
For extra flavor, add chickweed or mustard.

notes: Gather wild lettuce in early spring when plants are young.
Older plants get tough and wormy.
Wild lettuce has a milky juice when stems are broken.

recipes.title: Cochan (Tall Coneflower) Greens
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food recipe from Foxfire Book 2
recipes.description: Greens from the tall coneflower plant, parboiled and fried.

instructions.text: Pick cochan leaves when tender.
Parboil until tender.
Wash until water is clear.
Squeeze water out.
Put in pan with grease and fry.
Alternatively, after cooking, chop fine and add salt and margarine.
Top with chopped boiled eggs.

notes: Cochan grows along branch banks.
Looks like golden globe flowers.
Be careful not to confuse with wild parsnip, which has more whitish leaves.
Has a distinctive odor when cooking.

recipes.title: Tar Cough Syrup
recipes.source_note: Traditional home remedy from Foxfire Book 4
recipes.description: A traditional cough syrup made from pine tar, molasses, and sulfur.

instructions.text: Mix one part tar with five parts molasses and two parts sulfur.
Stir until well combined.
Take one teaspoonful at a time for coughs.

notes: Tar was also used on blisters, sores, and sometimes poison ivy.
Pine tar was traditionally melted from fat pine on a special rock.

flags: historical remedy - not for modern medical use

recipes.title: Sawmill Gravy
recipes.attribution: Traditional Appalachian logging camp, via Foxfire 4
recipes.source_note: Traditional breakfast gravy from Foxfire Book 4 logging camp section
recipes.description: Classic Appalachian white gravy made for logging camp breakfasts, served over biscuits.

instructions.text: Put flour in a great big skillet.
Let it brown a little bit in the pan drippings.
Dump in milk or water if you don't have milk.
Stir constantly until thickened.
Season with salt and pepper.
Serve over hot biscuits.

notes: Can be made with corn meal instead of flour.
Served every morning in logging camps with eggs, bacon, and biscuits.

recipes.title: Appalachian Ramp Soup
recipes.description: Traditional soup made with wild ramps, with three variations using beef or venison.

instructions.text: Cut one pound of beef in small pieces, add salt and water, and boil.
Skim the foam from the top.
Add ramps, carrots, and potatoes cut in small pieces.
Take out meat and eat separately.
Put vegetables through sieve and serve hot.

notes: Variation 1: Cook beef or venison and add celery leaves, bay leaves, three cloves, and thirty-six ramps. Take meat out and serve separately. Lift out ramps and serve broth with rice.
Variation 2: Add fried ramps to beef stock. Season with black pepper and serve.

recipes.title: Appalachian Ramp Salad
recipes.description: Fresh wild ramp salad with multiple serving variations.

instructions.text: Chop up young ramp leaves into tiny bits.
Eat raw, or cook and add vinegar when ready to eat.
Alternatively, add a little to any salad.
Or chop fine, parboil, drain and cool, and mix with mayonnaise and serve with trout.

notes: You can also add one-half cup chopped fine to mashed potatoes just before serving.

recipes.title: Mustard-Ramp Soup
recipes.description: Creamy soup made with wild mustard greens and ramps.

instructions.text: Clean and wash mustard leaves.
Heat one quart milk almost to boiling.
Meanwhile melt bacon fat in skillet, add chopped ramps, cook until brown.
Add salt, pepper, flour, and mustard. Cook five minutes.
Add milk and simmer.

recipes.title: Cooked Mustard Flowers
recipes.description: Simple preparation of wild mustard flowers.

instructions.text: Gather newly opened mustard blooms.
Cook in boiling water until tender.
Remove from heat, add butter or bacon fat.
Serve immediately.

recipes.title: Wild Garlic Vinegar
recipes.description: Infused vinegar made with wild garlic bulbs.

instructions.text: Peel garlic bulbs.
Place in one pint vinegar.
Cover tightly and let stand for ten to fourteen days.
Strain and bottle.

recipes.title: Blackberry Nectar
recipes.description: Sweet blackberry drink concentrate made with vinegar.

instructions.text: Select sound, ripe blackberries.
