recipes.description: Simple grilled eel with olive oil, paprika, and fresh sage.

instructions.text: Mix seasonings with oil; let sit 10 minutes.
Cut eel into 3-inch pieces; wipe dry.
Coat in oil mixture.
Broil 4 inches from heat or grill 10 minutes per side, basting with oil mixture.
Cook until light golden brown.

recipes.title: Jellied Eel
recipes.description: Traditional British jellied eel served cold.

instructions.text: Chop eels into 2-inch pieces.
Grease casserole with butter.
Combine all ingredients; season with salt.
Cover and bake at 325°F for one hour.
Cool, refrigerate overnight until liquid jellies.

recipes.title: English Eel Pie
recipes.description: Traditional English savory pie with eel, mushrooms, and sherry.

instructions.text: Cook eels with butter, mushrooms, parsley, onion, bay leaf, seasonings, lemon rind, Sherry, and stock until tender.
Strain sauce; thicken with butter and flour.
Line baking dish with pastry.
Add eels and sauce; top with egg slices.
Cover with pastry; brush with egg yolk.
Bake one hour at moderate temperature.
Serve hot or cold.

recipes.title: Achilles' Eel (Greek-Style)
recipes.description: Greek-style braised eel with tomatoes, feta, and herbs.

ingredients.prep_note: soaked in 2 tbsp boiling water, or 1 tbsp tomato paste

instructions.text: Heat oil in heavy skillet; brown eel pieces on all sides. Remove and set aside.
Add onions; fry until translucent.
Add sun-dried tomatoes (or paste), chopped tomatoes, honey, thyme, bay leaf, lemon zest, and garlic; simmer 10-12 minutes until sauce thickens.
Return eel; stir in parsley, mint, salt, and pepper.
Transfer to baking dish. Top with feta and sprinkle lemon juice.
Bake at 350°F for 30 minutes.

recipes.title: Gar Lobster
recipes.description: Boiled gar fish that tastes remarkably like lobster.

instructions.text: Prepare water with crab boil spices per package directions.
Add gar chunks to water (can wrap in cheesecloth).
Boil for 5 minutes or longer depending on quantity.
Turn off heat and let sit for same duration as boiling.
Drain meat thoroughly.
Dip each piece in melted butter and serve.

notes: Alternative: Dip nuggets in mustard and fry until golden
Never consume gar eggs or meat surrounding eggs

recipes.title: Cuy Chactado (Fried Guinea Pig)
recipes.description: Traditional Ayacucho-style fried guinea pig.

instructions.text: Pat the skin dry and rub with cumin, salt, and pepper.
Heat oil.
Dust the carcass with flour and place on its back in hot oil.
Turn to cook both sides until golden. Alternatively, cut into quarters before frying.
Serve with boiled potatoes or manioc root, plus a salad of tomatoes and slivered onions in lime juice and salt.

notes: Guinea pig has 21% protein and 8% fat - more protein and less cholesterol than beef, pork, or chicken

recipes.title: Cuy Picante Huanuqueño Style
recipes.description: Spicy Peruvian guinea pig with aji peppers and peanuts.

instructions.text: Quarter the guinea pigs and fry until golden brown.
In a heavy skillet, combine garlic, aji panca, and aji mirasol over high heat, stirring constantly.
Chop scallion bulbs and add with cumin.
Blend hearts, livers, and peanuts separately, then add to the pan.
Include guinea pig pieces and cook 10-15 minutes.
Let stand 15 minutes before serving over sliced potatoes.

recipes.title: Cuyes en Salsa de Maní (Guinea Pig with Peanut Sauce)
recipes.description: Deep-fried guinea pig served with creamy peanut sauce.

instructions.text: Season whole guinea pig with salt and pepper.
Deep fry in vegetable oil until golden and cooked through.
Serve with creamy peanut sauce, white rice, fried yuccas, and boiled sweet potatoes.

recipes.title: Garlic Mustard Vichyssoisse
recipes.description: A cold soup featuring foraged garlic mustard (jack-by-the-hedge) and three-cornered garlic.

instructions.text: In a heavy bottomed pan, add water and potatoes with a good pinch of salt. Boil until potatoes are soft. Remove from heat and set aside.
Melt butter in a medium saucepan. Add the onion and cook until softened. Pour over the boiled potatoes and water.
Blitz in food processor until smooth. Add water if needed to reach desired consistency. Pass through a sieve.
Chill in the refrigerator. Check seasoning.
Blanch jack-by-the-hedge for 10 seconds in salted boiling water and refresh in ice water.
Add jack-by-the-hedge and blitz again until smooth.
Add the three-cornered garlic, blitz until smooth, and check seasoning again.
Serve with crumbled goat's cheese, frothed milk, a pinch of cumin, crispy fried nettle dusted with white pepper, and a three-cornered garlic flower.

notes: Serve cold
Garlic mustard is also known as jack-by-the-hedge or sauce-alone

recipes.title: Sautéed Banana Tree Stem
recipes.description: A South Indian style preparation using the edible core of banana tree stems.

instructions.text: Remove outer fiber layer from banana stem and chop finely.
Wash and drain.
Heat half the oil; add mustard seeds until crackling.
Add chopped banana stem, curry leaves, salt, and chili powder. Optionally add turmeric for color.
Cover and simmer until soft, approximately one hour.
Blend grated coconut and garlic together.
Add coconut-garlic mixture when stem is nearly cooked; keep covered until fully cooked.
Drizzle remaining coconut oil over finished dish and mix.
Let sit covered briefly before serving.

notes: Use only the tender inner core of the banana stem

recipes.title: Roasted Bulrush Roots
recipes.description: Primitive pit-roasted bulrush roots wrapped in leaves.

instructions.text: Clean roots thoroughly, remove hair roots by scraping.
Wrap roots in large leaves.
Dig an 18-inch hole, 6 inches deep.
Build fire and create coal bed.
Place wrapped roots inside and cover with coals.
Roast for 2 to 3 hours.

notes: Traditional primitive cooking method

recipes.title: Bulrush Stew
recipes.description: A simple stew with bulrush roots and wild game.

instructions.text: Peel root skin and cut into inch-long pieces.
Boil with water, onions or mint, and meat for one hour.

notes: Traditional survival recipe

recipes.title: Bulrush Flour
recipes.description: How to make flour from dried bulrush roots.

instructions.text: Clean roots thoroughly.
Dry roots completely in sun.
Remove fibers.
Pound pulp into flour. The texture depends upon how much elbow grease you use.

notes: Can be used in place of regular flour in recipes

recipes.title: Bulrush Pancakes
recipes.description: Primitive pancakes made from bulrush root gruel.

instructions.text: Peel and cut roots.
Boil into gruel and let cool.
Mix with fat and meat.
Form into patties.
Fry on heated stones.

notes: Add berries for sweetness if desired

recipes.title: Bulrush Bread
recipes.description: Primitive bread made from bulrush root flour.

instructions.text: Skin and cut roots.
Boil into gruel.
Remove fibers.
Evaporate water to create sweet flour.
Mix with fat.
Roll onto flat rock and bake in reflector oven, or twist around stick and roast.

notes: The flour becomes naturally sweet as water evaporates

recipes.title: Fried Hornworms with Tomatoes and Basil
recipes.attribution: Eat the Weeds / David George Gordon
recipes.source_note: From eattheweeds.com - Tomato Tobacco Hornworms, credited to Eat-a-Bug Cookbook
recipes.description: Pan-fried tomato hornworms served atop fried green tomatoes with fresh basil.

instructions.text: Lightly fry the hornworms in a pan for a few minutes, being careful not to rupture the exoskeleton with high heat. Set aside to drain.
Sprinkle tomato slices with salt and pepper, then coat with cornmeal.
Fry tomato slices on both sides until lightly brown.
Top each tomato slice with one to two hornworms.
Crown each hornworm with a basil leaf.

notes: Hornworms should be purged (fed clean food) before cooking
Use low to medium heat to prevent rupturing

recipes.title: Classic Kamaro (Mole Cricket)
recipes.description: Traditional Filipino preparation of mole crickets, known as kamaro.

instructions.text: Boil the mole crickets in vinegar and garlic.
Drain the crickets.
Remove legs, wings, and claws.
Sauté the bodies in oil with chopped onion and tomatoes until they reach a chocolate brown color.
Serve with cold beer on the side.

notes: Result should be crispy on the outside, moist in the middle
A traditional Filipino delicacy from Pampanga province

recipes.title: Philippine-Style Kamaro (Adobo Style)
recipes.description: Mole crickets prepared adobo-style with soy sauce, vinegar, and optional coconut milk.

instructions.text: Numb the crickets and remove legs, wings, and claws.
Sauté crickets in garlic and onions.
Add soy sauce, vinegar, and hot pepper.
Optional: Add coconut milk to thicken the sauce.
Simmer until cooked through and sauce is reduced.

notes: Adobo-style preparation
Coconut milk adds richness

recipes.title: Euell Gibbons' Hawthorn Jelly
recipes.description: A classic hawthorn jelly recipe from foraging legend Euell Gibbons.

instructions.text: Crush three pounds of fruit.
Add water, bring to boil, cover and simmer 10 minutes.
Strain juice through jelly bag, discard pulp and seeds.
If fruit is overripe, add pectin; add lemon juice if desired.
Place 4 cups juice in large saucepan and bring to boil.
Add 7 cups sugar and return to boil.
Test for gel consistency and jar using standard canning methods.

notes: Euell Gibbons was a famous American forager and author
Pectin may not be needed if fruit is not overripe

recipes.title: Homemade Root Beer
recipes.source_note: From eattheweeds.com - Root Beer Rat Killer article comments
recipes.description: A traditional homemade root beer using foraged botanicals and natural ingredients.

instructions.text: Combine all ingredients in a large pot.
Boil together for 1 hour.
Strain the mixture through cheesecloth or fine mesh strainer.
Carbonate the strained liquid using your preferred method (natural fermentation with yeast or force carbonation).

notes: Traditional root beer uses sassafras which contains safrole - use sparingly or substitute sassafras flavoring
For natural carbonation, add champagne yeast and bottle in pressure-safe containers
Smilex is another name for sarsaparilla

recipes.title: Josep Mercader's Garum
recipes.description: A modern interpretation of ancient Roman garum using olives, anchovies, and fresh herbs.

ingredients.prep_note: soaked in water 1 hour, patted dry

instructions.text: Combine all ingredients in a blender or food processor.
Process until light and fluffy.
Pass mixture through a food mill or push through a sieve with a wooden spoon.
Return to blender or processor and briefly process until smooth.
Refrigerate until ready to use.

notes: Use fresh herbs only - do not substitute dried
Store refrigerated

recipes.title: Quick Garum
recipes.description: A quick approximation of ancient Roman garum using grape juice and anchovy paste.

instructions.text: Cook grape juice over medium heat, reducing to one-tenth its original volume (about 3/4 cup).
Dilute anchovy paste in the concentrated juice.
Mix in a pinch of oregano.

notes: A quick substitute for traditional fermented garum
Use as a savory condiment

recipes.title: Codium Salad
recipes.description: A refreshing raw seaweed salad with Asian-inspired dressing.

instructions.text: Mix all dressing ingredients (soy sauce, wine vinegar, sugar, sherry, and black pepper) together.
Pour the dressing over chopped onions.
Just before serving, chop the tomatoes and codium into bite-sized pieces.
Toss the chopped tomatoes and seaweed with the dressed onions.
Garnish with tomato slices.
Chill before serving.

notes: Never cook codium - it becomes soft and disintegrates from heat
Always eat raw after thorough washing

recipes.title: Sea Blite and Sour Cream Salad
recipes.description: A creamy salad featuring foraged sea blite with hard-boiled eggs.

ingredients.item: sea blite leaves, stems, or flowers

instructions.text: Cook sea blite in boiling water until tender, then drain and chop.
Combine all ingredients in a bowl and mix well.
Refrigerate for two hours before serving.

notes: Sea blite is naturally salty, so taste before adding salt
Also known as Suaeda

recipes.title: Garnished Sea Blite
recipes.description: Steamed sea blite topped with crispy bacon and Parmesan.

instructions.text: Boil or steam the sea blite until tender.
Drain thoroughly.
Combine with crispy bacon, cheese, vinegar, and bacon fat if desired.
Serve hot.

notes: A warm side dish featuring the naturally salty sea blite

recipes.title: Sea Blite Chicken Soup
recipes.description: A hearty chicken soup featuring foraged sea blite and Parmesan.

instructions.text: Boil chicken in water for 30 minutes.
Remove chicken and cut into bite-sized pieces.
Add all remaining ingredients except cheese to broth.
Simmer 45 minutes.
Return chicken to pot.
Stir in Parmesan cheese before serving.

notes: Sea blite adds natural saltiness - taste before adding salt

recipes.title: Lemongrass Tea (Knotted Blade Method)
recipes.description: A simple method for making fresh lemongrass tea using a knotted blade.

instructions.text: Take a complete lemongrass blade (be cautious, as the edges can cut you).
Starting from the bottom, begin tying the blade into knots.
Continue knotting until you have created a large knot with sufficient length remaining for a handle to dip with.
Place the knotted blade in hot water.
Allow to steep for one to two minutes.
Use the handle to stir if desired.

notes: The knotting releases more flavor than simply steeping a flat blade
Handle lemongrass carefully - blade edges are sharp

recipes.title: Molasses Sweet Bread
recipes.description: A moist, dark bread sweetened with sorghum molasses.

instructions.text: Mix flour, soda, and salt.
Combine molasses, buttermilk, egg, and melted butter.
Add liquid ingredients to dry, mix just until combined.
Pour into greased loaf pan.
Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 50-60 minutes until done.

notes: Sorghum molasses gives the most authentic flavor
Keeps well when wrapped

recipes.title: Carrot Pudding
recipes.source_note: Traditional steamed pudding from Foxfire collection
recipes.description: A moist, spiced steamed pudding made with grated carrots.

instructions.text: Mix grated carrots and potatoes with melted butter.
Sift together flour, sugar, soda, and spices.
Add dry ingredients to carrot mixture.
Fold in raisins.
Pour into greased pudding mold or can.
Steam for 2 hours.
Serve warm with hard sauce or cream.

notes: Can be made ahead and resteamed to serve
Traditional Christmas dessert

recipes.title: Dried Apple Cake
recipes.source_note: Traditional cake using preserved dried apples
recipes.description: A dense, moist spice cake made with reconstituted dried apples.

instructions.text: Soak dried apples in water overnight, then cook until soft. Drain and mash.
While hot, stir in molasses. Let cool.
Cream butter and sugar, add eggs.
Sift flour with soda and spices.
Add flour mixture alternately with buttermilk.
Fold in apple mixture.
Pour into greased tube pan.
Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 45-50 minutes.

notes: Dried apples were preserved each fall for winter baking
Very moist - keeps well

recipes.title: Tame Gooseberry Pie
recipes.description: A sweet-tart pie made with tame (cultivated) gooseberries.

instructions.text: Wash gooseberries and remove stems and blossom ends.
Mix sugar and flour, toss with berries.
Pour into pastry-lined pie plate.
Dot with butter.
Cover with top crust, seal and flute edges, cut vents.
Bake at 425°F (220°C) for 15 minutes, reduce to 350°F (175°C) for 30 minutes more.

notes: 'Tame' refers to cultivated berries vs wild ones
Tart and refreshing

recipes.title: Rose Hip Tea
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian medicinal tea from wild roses
recipes.description: A vitamin C-rich tea made from rose hips, with a flavor similar to apples.

instructions.text: Cook rose hips in water until soft.
Strain off the juice.
Reheat juice with honey or sugar to taste.
Serve hot. Tastes similar to apple.

notes: Darker hips make better tea
Rose hips are very high in vitamin C
Harvest after first frost for best flavor

recipes.title: Rose Hip Jelly
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian jelly from wild rose hips
recipes.description: A delicate jelly made from wild rose hips, high in vitamin C.

instructions.text: Put rose hips in boiler with water.
Simmer until soft, then strain juice.
Let juice start simmering, add one cup sugar per cup juice.
Boil until jelly stage is reached.
Pour into jars and set in dark place to thicken.

notes: Can substitute haws (hawthorn berries) for rose hips
High in vitamin C

recipes.title: Scuppernong Preserves
recipes.description: Sweet preserves made from scuppernong grapes, a native Southern muscadine variety.

instructions.text: Cook grapes until seeds come free.
Strain through sieve or colander.
Add half cup sugar per cup juice.
Cook until mixture jellies.
Pack in hot jars and seal.

notes: For spiced preserves, add cinnamon, mace, and one cup vinegar
Scuppernongs are bronze-colored muscadine grapes native to the South

recipes.title: Scuppernong Pie
recipes.description: A unique Southern pie made with native scuppernong grapes.

instructions.text: Heat grapes in saucepan.
Add salt, then cream together butter, sugar, flour, and egg.
Pour butter mixture over grapes.
Pour all into uncooked pie shell.
Lattice top with pastry strips.
Bake one hour at 300°F (150°C).

notes: Scuppernongs must be seeded before using
Low and slow baking creates best texture

recipes.title: Cattail Pancakes
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food pancakes from cattail roots
recipes.description: Pancakes made from cattail root gruel, served with wild berries or stewed apples.

instructions.text: Boil cattail roots into a gruel consistency.
Drain and dry the gruel.
Mix with egg, milk, salt, and margarine.
Drop by tablespoons into well-greased cast-iron skillet.
Cook until browned on both sides.
Serve with cooked blueberries or stewed apples.

notes: Cattail roots are best harvested in fall or early spring
Also called 'nature's grocery store' due to many edible parts

recipes.title: Cattail Pollen Flapjacks
recipes.source_note: Traditional wild food flapjacks using cattail pollen
recipes.description: Golden flapjacks made with nutritious cattail pollen.

instructions.text: Mix pollen, flour, baking powder, and salt together.
Beat eggs and add to dry ingredients with milk, water, and sugar.
Add bacon drippings and mix well.
Fry in greased pan until golden brown on both sides.

notes: Collect pollen in late spring when cattail heads are bright yellow
Pollen adds golden color and mild flavor

recipes.title: Hawthorn (Red Haw) Jelly
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian jelly from hawthorn berries
recipes.description: A brown-colored jelly from hawthorn berries that tastes similar to guava.

instructions.text: Simmer haws in water until soft.
Mash the berries and strain through jelly bag.
Add one pound sugar per pint of liquid plus a dash of lemon juice.
Boil until jelly stage is reached.
Pour into jars and seal.

notes: Results in a brown jelly tasting like guava
Haws are also called thornapples

recipes.title: Maypop Jelly
recipes.source_note: Traditional jelly from wild passionflower fruit
recipes.description: A delicate jelly made from maypops (wild passionflower fruit).

instructions.text: Use the seeds and pulp of ripe maypops.
Boil for 15 minutes in water.
Strain through jelly bag.
Add one pint sugar per pint juice.
Boil 25-30 minutes until mixture jellies.
Pour into jars and seal.

notes: For syrup, boil only until thin syrup - good with biscuits or pancakes
Maypops are wild passionflower fruit native to the Southeast

recipes.title: Jerusalem Artichoke Pickle
recipes.description: A spiced pickle made from Jerusalem artichokes (sunchokes).

instructions.text: Peel artichokes and slice. Sprinkle well with salt.
Slice onions and salt them as well.
Let stand 24 hours, then wash off salt well.
Boil vinegar, sugar, and spices for 10 minutes.
Add onions and artichokes and boil 10 minutes more.
Seal in hot jars.

notes: Jerusalem artichokes are also called sunchokes
Some add horseradish instead of other spices

recipes.title: Pumpkin Butter
recipes.description: A smooth, spiced spread made from cooked pumpkin, similar to apple butter.

instructions.text: Cut and peel pumpkin.
Cook pumpkin thoroughly until very soft.
Mash until smooth.
Add sugar and cinnamon to taste.
Cook down until thick and spreadable.
Pour into jars and seal.

notes: Can use pie pumpkins or butternut squash
Makes excellent toast or biscuit spread

recipes.title: Quince Honey
recipes.description: A sweet preserve made from grated quinces cooked in sugar syrup.

instructions.text: Grate the quinces.
Boil sugar and water together to make syrup.
Add grated quinces to the syrup.
Boil for twenty minutes.
Seal in jars.

notes: The same method works for pear honey
Quinces must be cooked - too hard and tart to eat raw

recipes.title: Raspberry Jelly
recipes.description: A bright, flavorful jelly made from wild raspberries.

instructions.text: Boil raspberries in water until cooked.
Strain through jelly bag.
Add one pound sugar per pint of juice.
Boil until mixture sets.
Pour into jars and seal.

notes: Wild raspberries have more intense flavor than cultivated
Works with black or red raspberries

recipes.title: Raspberry Preserves
recipes.description: Thick preserves made from nearly-ripe raspberries.

instructions.text: Gather nearly-ripe berries.
Boil berries with water for ten minutes.
Drain off two-thirds of the juice.
Add one pound sugar per pound of berries.
Boil until thick.
Pour into jars and seal.

notes: Nearly-ripe berries hold their shape better
Save the drained juice for other uses

recipes.title: Blackberry Syrup
recipes.source_note: Traditional spiced blackberry syrup for pancakes
recipes.description: A spiced syrup made from blackberry juice, perfect for pancakes.

instructions.text: Cook blackberries and strain to get juice.
Mix juice with sugar and all spices.
Boil for 15 minutes.
Pour into bottles and seal.
Serve over pancakes.

notes: Adjust spices to taste
Also good over waffles or ice cream

recipes.title: Blackberry Flummery
recipes.description: A chilled fruit pudding thickened with cornstarch, a traditional English-American dessert.

instructions.text: Cook berries with water, sugar, salt, and cinnamon until syrupy.
Mix cornstarch with a little cold water to make a paste.
Stir cornstarch paste into berry mixture.
Simmer until thick.
Chill before serving.

notes: Flummery is an old English dessert brought to Appalachia
Serve with cream if desired

recipes.title: Blackberry Roll
recipes.description: A rolled biscuit dough filled with blackberries and honey, baked in a pool of berries.

instructions.text: Roll biscuit dough to 1/3-inch thickness.
Brush with softened butter.
Mix half the berries with cinnamon and honey, spread on dough.
Roll up like a jelly roll.
Place in baking pan surrounded by remaining berries mixed with sugar.
Bake 30 minutes at 425°F (220°C).

notes: The surrounding berries create a sauce while baking
Serve warm with cream

recipes.title: Blackberry Cordial
recipes.description: A spiced blackberry liqueur traditionally used for medicinal purposes.

instructions.text: Boil berries in water until soft.
Strain through cloth.
To one pint juice add one pound sugar, mace, and cloves.
Boil for 15 minutes.
Cool and strain again.
Add 3/4 cup whiskey per quart.
Bottle and seal.

notes: Traditionally used for stomach ailments
Can substitute brandy for whiskey

recipes.title: Wild Blueberry Cobbler
recipes.description: A rustic cobbler made with wild blueberries and biscuit-style topping.

instructions.text: Cook berries 15 minutes over medium heat with sugar.
Make dough with flour and shortening, roll thin.
Cut dough into pieces and place on top of berries.
Boil briefly, then bake until crust browns.

notes: Wild blueberries are smaller but more flavorful
Serve warm with cream

recipes.title: Blueberry Fritters
recipes.description: Light, fried dough balls studded with blueberries and dusted with sugar.

instructions.text: Mix biscuit dough with beaten egg and sugar.
Fold in blueberries.
Heat grease in deep pan.
Drop batter by spoonfuls into hot grease.
Turn until brown on all sides.
Drain and sprinkle with sugar.

notes: Don't crowd the pan - fry in batches
Serve immediately while hot

recipes.title: Blueberry Crisp
recipes.description: Fresh blueberries topped with a buttery oat crumble.

instructions.text: Place blueberries in baking dish and toss with white sugar.
Cream butter with brown sugar.
Blend in flour and oats.
Spread topping over berries.
Bake until topping is golden and berries bubble.

notes: Can add a pinch of cinnamon to topping
Serve warm with vanilla ice cream

recipes.title: Huckleberry Cake
recipes.description: A rich butter cake loaded with wild huckleberries.

instructions.text: Cream butter with sugar.
Add flour alternately with egg yolks.
Add milk, baking powder, and vanilla.
Fold in huckleberries.
Bake in loaf pan at 350°F for 45 minutes to one hour.

notes: Wild huckleberries have more intense flavor than blueberries
Toss berries in a little flour to prevent sinking

recipes.title: Huckleberry Jam
recipes.description: A thick, flavorful jam made from wild huckleberries.

instructions.text: Wash berries and place in pot with water.
Boil until very tender.
Add half pound sugar per pound fruit.
Boil 30 minutes until thick.
Pour into jars and seal.

notes: Huckleberries are found in mountain forests
Jam thickens more as it cools

recipes.title: Elderberry Pie
recipes.description: A deep purple pie made with wild elderberries.

instructions.text: Make thin pastry crust and bake before adding filling.
Mix elderberries with cornstarch and sugar.
Pour into cooked crust.
Bake 30 minutes at 325°F (165°C).

notes: Never eat red elderberries - only black/blue varieties are safe
Pre-baking the crust prevents soggy bottom

recipes.title: Elderflower Flapjacks
recipes.description: Delicate pancakes made with fragrant elderflower blossoms.

instructions.text: Remove stems from flower clusters.
Wash flowers in one quart water with salt.
Mix flowers with pancake batter.
Fry until golden on both sides.
Sprinkle with sugar and serve.

notes: Harvest elderflowers in late spring when fragrant
The salt wash removes any insects

recipes.title: Elderberry Wine
recipes.description: A deep red wine made from wild elderberries, a traditional Appalachian beverage.

instructions.text: Mash berries in a crock.
Add water and stir daily for two weeks.
Strain through cloth.
Add equal amount of sugar to juice.
Stand two more weeks, stirring occasionally.
Bottle when fermentation stops.

notes: Only use black or blue elderberries - red elderberries are toxic
Store in cool, dark place after bottling

recipes.title: Fig Preserves
recipes.description: Sweet whole fig preserves, a Southern delicacy.

instructions.text: Wash figs and pat dry.
Bring sugar and water to a boil, add figs.
Cook slowly until tender, let stand overnight.
Day 2: Drain syrup, boil again, pour over figs, stand overnight.
Day 3: Cook figs in syrup until clear, add lemon juice.
Pack in jars and process 30 minutes in hot water bath.

notes: The multi-day process keeps figs whole and plump
Use firm ripe figs for best results

recipes.title: Wild Grape Jelly
recipes.description: A flavorful jelly made from wild grapes with a hint of vinegar.

instructions.text: Wash grapes and remove stems.
Crush grapes in large pan.
Add vinegar and cinnamon if desired.
Cook slowly 15 minutes, then strain through cheesecloth.
Boil juice 20 minutes, add sugar.
Cook until starts to jell, pour into jars.

notes: Fox grapes, possum grapes, or muscadines all work
The vinegar adds brightness and helps preserve

recipes.title: Wild Grape Juice
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian grape juice for canning
recipes.description: A simple method for making and preserving wild grape juice.

instructions.text: Sterilize quart jars.
Place two cups washed fully ripe grapes in each jar.
Add half cup sugar.
Fill to top with boiling water.
Seal immediately.
Stand 3-4 weeks before straining for use.

notes: The grapes steep and release their juice over time
Strain before serving

recipes.title: Spiced Wild Grapes
recipes.description: Wild grapes preserved in a sweet, spiced vinegar syrup.

instructions.text: Wash and stem grapes.
Pulp grapes (squeeze pulp from skins).
Put pulp with seeds over fire, cook until seeds come free.
Add skins and pulp with sugar, vinegar, and spices.
Cook until thick.
Can while hot.

notes: Pulping separates the skins from the seedy centers
Excellent with game meats

recipes.title: Muscadine Jelly
recipes.description: A classic Southern jelly made from half-ripe muscadine grapes.

instructions.text: Take pulp and juice of half-ripe muscadines.
Nearly cover with water and boil few minutes.
Strain through jelly bag.
Measure juice and add one pound white sugar per pint juice.
Boil until congeals when dropped on cold dry surface (20-30 minutes).

notes: Half-ripe grapes have more pectin for better jelling
Test by dropping on cold plate

recipes.title: Wild Grape Wine
recipes.description: A simple homemade wine from wild grapes.

instructions.text: Crush grapes and mix with sugar in large crock or barrel.
Let work nine days, stirring daily.
Strain through cloth.
Let work nine more days.
Strain again and seal loosely in jars.
When completely done working, seal tightly and store in dark place.

notes: Don't seal too tight during fermentation or jars may explode
Patience improves the wine

recipes.title: Cranberry Sauce
recipes.description: A simple two-ingredient cranberry sauce.

instructions.text: Wash berries.
Add sugar to berries, stirring thoroughly.
Cook slowly without additional water (just what remains from washing).
Boil for 10 minutes.

notes: No additional water needed - the washing water is sufficient

recipes.title: Spiced Cranberries
recipes.description: Tangy spiced cranberries preserved in vinegar with warm spices.

instructions.text: Combine all ingredients in a large pot.
Boil for 2 hours.
Place in hot sterilized jars and seal.

notes: For canning - use proper canning procedures

recipes.title: Cranberry Orange Relish
recipes.description: A fresh, no-cook cranberry orange relish.

instructions.text: Put berries and oranges (including rind) through food grinder using coarse blade.
Stir in sugar.
Chill before serving.

notes: Keeps several weeks refrigerated
Include the orange rind for best flavor

recipes.title: Cranberry Punch
recipes.description: A festive cranberry punch with citrus and ginger ale.

instructions.text: Cook berries in 4 cups water until soft.
Crush and drain through cheesecloth.
Boil sugar and remaining 2 cups water for 5 minutes.
Add sugar syrup to berry juice and chill.
Add orange juice and lemon juice.
Just before serving, add ginger ale.

notes: Add ginger ale just before serving to keep it fizzy

recipes.title: Cranberry Salsa
recipes.description: A unique cranberry salsa with cilantro, jalapeño, and lime.

instructions.text: Combine all ingredients in food processor fitted with medium blade.
Chop to medium consistency.
Refrigerate if not using immediately.
Serve at room temperature.

notes: Great with tortilla chips or as a topping for turkey

recipes.title: Cranberry Muffins
recipes.description: Hearty whole wheat and oat muffins studded with cranberries.

instructions.text: Combine milk and oats and let stand.
Mix egg, oil, and brown sugar together.
Mix dry ingredients (flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt).
Add berries to dry ingredients and toss until coated.
Mix all ingredients together just until blended.
Fill greased muffin cups.
Bake at 350°F for 18-20 minutes.

notes: Sour the milk by adding 1 tbsp lemon juice or vinegar
Don't overmix the batter

recipes.title: Lemon Grass Dog (Vietnamese Style)
recipes.source_note: From eattheweeds.com - Dog and Cat article (historical/cultural recipe)
recipes.description: A traditional Vietnamese preparation using lemongrass marinade. Dog meat is consumed in parts of Asia.

instructions.text: Mince four 3-foot stalks of fresh lemongrass (or use 8 oz frozen minced lemongrass).
Mix minced lemongrass with fish sauce, lime juice, and lime zest.
Chop meat into 1-inch pieces.
Add lemongrass marinade to meat and stir well.
Refrigerate mixture overnight.
Sauté, steam, or grill the meat. Alternatively, skewer chunks and roast in rotisserie oven.
Serve with jasmine rice, rice vermicelli, or baguette.

notes: Historical/cultural recipe from Vietnam
Dog meat consumption is traditional in parts of Asia

recipes.title: Cat Braisé (French Style)
recipes.source_note: From eattheweeds.com - Dog and Cat article (historical recipe)
recipes.description: A historical French-style braised preparation with artichokes and white wine. Cat was historically consumed during times of scarcity.

ingredients.prep_note: cut into serving pieces, dusted with flour, salt, and pepper

instructions.text: Prepare artichokes by snapping off outer leaves; trim stems and remove chokes; cut bottoms into quarters and soak in lemon-water.
Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in large casserole; brown seasoned meat pieces on all sides; remove to plate.
Discard remaining oil; add 1 tbsp fresh oil and bacon; sauté until cooked.
Add remaining oil, onion, and carrot; sauté 5 minutes.
Add artichoke quarters and garlic; stir 1 minute; add tomatoes and white wine.
Reduce heat until syrupy, stirring constantly, approximately 5 minutes.
Lay bouquet garni over vegetables; arrange meat pieces on top with accumulated juices.
Pour broth halfway up meat pieces; cover and simmer 1 hour or bake at 350°F for 1 hour.
Meat should be tender; turn pieces once during cooking.
Remove meat pieces and vegetables to warm platter; strain pan juices, reduce by one-third, and pour over.
Serve immediately; garnish with parsley if desired.

notes: Historical recipe - cat was consumed during wartime and famine in Europe
French braising technique

recipes.title: Fried Acorn Grubs
recipes.description: Simple fried grubs - soft and buttery when cooked properly.

instructions.text: Heat butter or oil over LOW heat. This is critical.
Add grubs and fry gently for a few minutes.
Do NOT use high heat - grubs will explode within a second in very hot fat.
Cook until soft and buttery.

notes: Raw grubs taste mild and chewy like fat
Cooked grubs are soft and buttery
Peak harvest is September after August rains

recipes.title: New Jersey Tea
recipes.description: Revolutionary War-era tea substitute made from Red Root plant.

instructions.text: Hand-crush leaves slightly.
If using fresh leaves, shade dry them first.
Steep in hot water like black tea.
Use 1 tablespoon fresh leaves OR 1 teaspoon dried leaves per cup.

notes: Colonial fermentation method: Make a decoction of leaves and twigs, dip fresh leaves in it, then dry
Best harvest time is early summer when plant blossoms
Seeds are NOT edible

recipes.title: Tonburi (Land Caviar from Kochia Seeds)
recipes.description: Japanese preparation of kochia seeds that resemble caviar.

instructions.text: Dry the seeds thoroughly.
Boil the dried seeds.
Soak in cold water for one full day.
Rub seeds by hand to remove outer skin.
Seeds will become glossy black-green and resemble caviar.

notes: Used as garnish in Japanese cuisine
Plant is very salty tasting
Like spinach, kochia can accumulate nitrates

recipes.title: Puffball Crepes
recipes.description: Thin-sliced puffball mushrooms used like crepes.

instructions.text: CRITICAL: Cut puffball from top to bottom and examine inside.
Interior must be marshmallow soft, pure white (never dark), with thin outer skin and no outline of mushroom inside.
Slice puffball very thin.
Brown slices with butter in a pan.
Use like crepes - fill and roll.

notes: Puffballs absorb flavor well but have little taste on their own
DANGER: Young Amanita (deadly) can look like small puffballs - always cut open to verify
Young Scleroderma (fatal) has hard white flesh inside

recipes.title: Breaded Deep-Fried Puffball
recipes.description: Puffball slices breaded and deep fried like potatoes.

instructions.text: Verify puffball safety: cut open, check for pure white, soft interior with no mushroom outline.
Slice like potatoes.
Bread slices in flour.
Deep fry until golden.

notes: Can also cube for miso soup or cut into strips for stir fry

recipes.title: Water Hyacinth Stir Fry
recipes.description: Deep fried water hyacinth bulbs and steamed leaves.

instructions.text: Harvest only from clean water sources - never downstream from mines.
Deep fry young bulbous bottoms in butter until crispy like pork rinds.
Steam young leaves like mustard greens with bacon or pork fat.
Alternatively, boil or fry leaves.

notes: May cause itching in some people even when cooked
Contains 18.7% protein
ILLEGAL to collect/possess in Florida
Flowers can be boiled or candied

recipes.title: Coquina Beach Chowder
recipes.description: A foraged beach chowder using coquina clams and sea purslane.

instructions.text: Boil coquina clams and mole crabs together for broth.
Cook sea purslane separately in plain water to reduce its natural salt.
Combine broth with purslane and some coquina meat.
Warm together and serve.
Add butter and cream if available for richer chowder.

notes: Coquina broth also makes excellent base for creamed potato soup
Can stuff fish with sea purslane or sea rocket

recipes.title: Fried Palmetto Weevil Grubs (Grugru)
recipes.source_note: From eattheweeds.com - Palmetto Weevil Grub article
recipes.description: Fried palm grubs - a tropical delicacy.

instructions.text: Slice or crack grub partway open around the middle.
This prevents explosion during cooking.
Fry in oil or butter until cooked through.
Alternatively, roast next to an open fire.

notes: Can also be eaten raw
Pupa stage is reportedly tastiest but rarest
Contains 3-7% protein and 10-30% fat
Find in dying palms with dead/bent growing tips

recipes.title: Sunflower Hull Coffee
recipes.description: A coffee substitute made from roasted sunflower seed hulls.

instructions.text: Collect sunflower seed hulls.
Roast hulls until dark and fragrant.
Brew roasted hulls in hot water like coffee.

notes: Seeds can be roasted for snacks or ground raw to thicken soups
Young stems can be roasted
Inner stalk pulp was chewed as gum by Pima Indians

recipes.title: Agave Flowers with Scrambled Eggs (Oaxacan Style)
recipes.description: Traditional Oaxacan preparation of agave flowers.

instructions.text: Harvest flowers during summer bloom.
Boil flowers until tender.
Mix boiled flowers with scrambled eggs.
Cook together until eggs are set.

notes: Flowers can also be roasted
WARNING: Raw agave juice causes dermatitis - wear eye protection when cutting
Avoid Agave lechuguilla (toxic species in TX/NM)

recipes.title: Pit-Roasted Agave Heart
recipes.description: Traditional pit-baked agave stalk with molasses-like flavor.

instructions.text: Harvest stalk before the plant blooms in summer.
Dig a pit and line with rocks.
Build fire and reduce to ashes/coals.
Place agave heart inside pit.
Cover to retain heat.
Retrieve next day after 24 hours.

notes: Tastes like molasses when roasted
Old and tough plants are best (opposite of typical foraging)
Seeds can be ground into flour for bread or soup thickener

recipes.title: Wild Potato Vine Root (Ipomoea pandurata)
recipes.description: Wild tuber that must be boiled twice to remove acridity.

instructions.text: Cube the roots.
Boil in water until tender.
DRAIN and discard water.
Boil again in fresh water.
Optionally roast the cubes after double-boiling.

notes: NEVER eat raw
Must boil in at least two changes of water
Younger/smaller roots are less acrid than older ones
Roots grow straight down from vine entry point

recipes.title: Water Spinach Stir Fry
recipes.description: Simple Asian-style stir fried water spinach.

instructions.text: Heat oil in wok or pan.
Add garlic and stir fry briefly.
Add water spinach shoots and leaves.
Stir fry until wilted.
Season with salt.

notes: Can be eaten raw from clean water
48% carbs, 24% protein
Rich in vitamins A, C, E

recipes.title: Jerusalem Artichoke Pickles
recipes.description: Pickled sunchokes using bread and butter pickle method.

instructions.text: Clean tubers thoroughly - they are lumpy and tedious.
Slice tubers.
Pickle using bread and butter style method (works better than dill).

notes: Pick tubers two weeks after flowers fade
Flavor improves after frost
Don't store except in ground - dig as needed
Build digestive tolerance by eating small portions for 3-4 days first

recipes.title: Popped Wild Rice with Maple Sugar
recipes.description: Traditional Ojibwa preparation of popped wild rice.

instructions.text: Heat a dry pan.
Add parched wild rice grains.
Pop like popcorn, stirring constantly.
Mix with maple sugar or leftover maple syrup solids.

notes: Harvest mid-August to mid-September when plants still green
Sun dry at least 2 days before parching
Hull immediately after parching or grains reabsorb moisture
Keep away from sand

recipes.title: Poplar Bark Bread
recipes.source_note: From eattheweeds.com - Poplars and Aspens article
recipes.description: Survival bread made with dried poplar inner bark.

instructions.text: Cut inner bark (cambium) into strips.
Dry strips completely.
Grind dried bark into powder.
Mix bark powder with regular flour.
Add water to form dough and bake as bread, or cook as mush.

notes: Inner bark is edible raw or cooked
High in Vitamin C
Best species: Eastern Cottonwood, Fremont Cottonwood, Aspens
Twigs have bitter aspirin-like taste

recipes.title: Elder Blow Champagne
recipes.source_note: From eattheweeds.com - Edible Flowers Part Three
recipes.description: Light sparkling wine flavored with elderberry blossoms.

instructions.text: Harvest elderberry blossoms when fully open.
Use blossoms to flavor light summer wine.
Allow to ferment to sparkling stage.

notes: Elderberry blossoms can also be added to pancake batter
Use only true elderberry - not water elder or other lookalikes

recipes.title: Linden-Basswood Tea
recipes.source_note: From eattheweeds.com - Edible Flowers Part Three
recipes.description: Honey-flavored tea from linden/basswood blossoms.

instructions.text: Harvest and dry linden/basswood blossoms.
Steep dried blossoms in hot water.
Strain and serve.

notes: Has natural honey flavor
Mix blossoms with basswood seeds for chocolate-like taste

recipes.title: Wokas (Yellow Pond Lily Seeds)
recipes.source_note: From eattheweeds.com - Yellow Pond Lily article
recipes.description: Traditional Native American preparation of pond lily seeds.

instructions.text: Collect ripe seed pods.
Place in water for EXACTLY three weeks - this removes bitterness through enzyme action.
Remove seeds from rotted pods.
Air dry seeds completely.
Pop like popcorn (they crack rather than puff), or grind into flour.

notes: Seeds can be stored as staple or used to thicken soups
Roots are NOT recommended - extremely bitter even after extensive processing
Young leaves can go in soups but may be bitter

recipes.title: High Bush Cranberry Flower Fritters
recipes.source_note: From eattheweeds.com - High Bush Cranberry article
recipes.description: Flowers dipped in pancake batter and fried.

instructions.text: Harvest high bush cranberry flowers.
Dip flowers in pancake batter.
Fry until golden and batter is cooked through.

notes: Berries taste better after one or two frosts
Berries make excellent jelly without added pectin
Use orange zest to enhance berry flavor

recipes.title: Spicebush Tea
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: A warming tea made from spicebush twigs, popular as a spring tonic.

instructions.text: Gather young spicebush twigs in early spring.
Break twigs into small pieces and place in pot.
Cover with water and bring to a boil.
Simmer for 10-15 minutes until fragrant.
Strain and sweeten with honey if desired.

notes: Also known as 'poor man's allspice' due to its aromatic flavor

recipes.title: Sweet Birch Tea
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: A wintergreen-flavored tea from sweet birch twigs.

instructions.text: Collect young sweet birch twigs.
Chop or break into small pieces.
Place in pot and cover with cold water.
Bring slowly to a simmer (do not boil vigorously).
Steep for 10 minutes, strain and serve.

notes: Has a natural wintergreen flavor
Best gathered in early spring when sap is running

recipes.title: Birch Beer
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: Traditional fermented beverage made from birch sap and twigs.

ingredients.item: birch sap or strong birch twig tea

instructions.text: Make a strong tea from birch twigs or collect birch sap in early spring.
Dissolve sugar in warm birch liquid.
Cool to lukewarm and add yeast.
Cover and let ferment for 2-3 days.
Bottle and refrigerate. Drink within a week.

notes: A mildly fermented, refreshing spring beverage

recipes.title: Fried Morels
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: Simple pan-fried morel mushrooms, a springtime delicacy.

instructions.text: Clean morels by soaking briefly in salted water to remove insects.
Slice larger morels in half lengthwise.
Melt butter in skillet over medium heat.
Add morels and sauté until golden, about 5-7 minutes.
Season with salt and pepper and serve immediately.

notes: Always positively identify morels - never eat wild mushrooms unless certain

recipes.title: Stuffed Morels
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: Morel mushrooms stuffed with a savory sausage filling.

instructions.text: Clean morels carefully, keeping them whole.
Brown sausage with onion; drain fat.
Mix sausage with cream cheese and bread crumbs.
Stuff mixture into morel cavities.
Bake at 350°F for 15-20 minutes until heated through.

notes: Can substitute other mild cheese for cream cheese

recipes.title: Ramp Soup
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: A simple, flavorful soup made with wild ramps.

instructions.text: Sauté ramps in butter until softened.
Add potatoes and broth; simmer until potatoes are tender.
Mash some potatoes against side of pot to thicken.
Stir in cream and season to taste.
Serve hot.

notes: Ramps have a strong garlic-onion flavor
Available only in early spring

recipes.title: Fried Ramps with Eggs
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: Traditional Appalachian breakfast of fried ramps with scrambled eggs.

instructions.text: Separate ramp bulbs from leaves; slice bulbs.
Fry bulbs in bacon drippings until softened.
Add chopped leaves and cook briefly.
Beat eggs and pour over ramps.
Scramble until eggs are set. Season and serve.

notes: A beloved spring tradition in Appalachia

recipes.title: Cattail Pollen Flapjacks
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: Golden pancakes using wild cattail pollen as flour.

instructions.text: Mix pollen, flour, baking powder, and salt.
Beat egg with milk and melted butter.
Stir wet ingredients into dry just until combined.
Pour onto hot greased griddle.
Cook until bubbles form; flip and cook until golden.

notes: Collect pollen in early summer when cattail heads are bright yellow

recipes.title: Hickory Nut Cake
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: Rich layer cake studded with native hickory nuts.

instructions.text: Cream butter and sugar; beat in eggs one at a time.
Mix flour and baking powder.
Add dry ingredients alternately with milk; stir in vanilla.
Fold in hickory nuts.
Pour into 2 greased 9-inch pans. Bake at 350°F for 30-35 minutes.

notes: Hickory nuts have rich, buttery flavor similar to pecans

recipes.title: Hickory Nut Pie
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: Similar to pecan pie but made with foraged hickory nuts.

instructions.text: Beat eggs; stir in sugar, corn syrup, butter, and vanilla.
Spread hickory nuts in pie shell.
Pour filling over nuts.
Bake at 350°F for 50-60 minutes until set.

notes: Cover edges with foil if browning too quickly

recipes.title: Wild Hazelnut Cookies
recipes.attribution: Foxfire Book of Wild Plant Foods
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Wild Plant Foods
recipes.description: Crisp butter cookies with toasted wild hazelnuts.

instructions.text: Cream butter and sugars; beat in egg.
Mix flour and baking soda; stir into creamed mixture.
Fold in hazelnuts.
Drop by spoonfuls onto greased baking sheet.
Bake at 375°F for 10-12 minutes until edges are golden.

notes: Toast hazelnuts in dry skillet to enhance flavor

recipes.title: Roast Bear
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Meats and Small Game
recipes.description: Traditional slow-roasted bear with vegetables.

instructions.text: Remove all fat from bear meat (fat can be strong-tasting).
Season roast with salt and pepper.
Brown on all sides in hot Dutch oven.
Add vegetables and broth.
Cover and roast at 325°F for 3-4 hours until very tender.

notes: Bear must be cooked well-done to kill trichinella parasites
Remove all fat before cooking

recipes.title: Pan-Fried Venison Steaks
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Meats and Small Game
recipes.description: Quick-cooked tender venison steaks.

instructions.text: Pound steaks lightly to tenderize.
Season flour with salt and pepper; dredge steaks.
Heat drippings in heavy skillet over medium-high heat.
Cook steaks 3-4 minutes per side for medium-rare.
Do not overcook - venison becomes tough when well-done.

notes: Venison is lean - cook quickly and don't overcook

recipes.title: Venison Pot Roast
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Meats and Small Game
recipes.description: Tender braised venison roast with gravy.

instructions.text: Lay bacon strips over top of roast (adds fat venison lacks).
Brown roast on all sides in Dutch oven.
Add onion, broth, bay leaves, and seasonings.
Cover and simmer on stovetop or bake at 300°F for 3 hours.
Remove roast; thicken pan juices for gravy.

notes: Adding bacon or salt pork provides fat that lean venison lacks

recipes.title: Roasted Quail
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Meats and Small Game
recipes.description: Simple roasted quail wrapped in bacon.

instructions.text: Season quail inside and out with salt and pepper.
Place 1 tbsp butter inside each bird.
Wrap 2 bacon strips around each quail.
Place in baking dish.
Roast at 400°F for 25-30 minutes until juices run clear.

notes: Allow 1-2 quail per person depending on size

recipes.title: Roast Wild Turkey
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Meats and Small Game
recipes.description: Moist roasted wild turkey with traditional dressing.

instructions.text: Rub turkey inside and out with salt, pepper, and butter.
Lay bacon strips over breast.
Place in roasting pan with broth.
Roast at 325°F, basting frequently, about 20 min per pound.
Remove bacon last 30 minutes to brown skin.

notes: Wild turkey is leaner than domestic - baste frequently and don't overcook

recipes.title: Turtle Stew
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Meats and Small Game
recipes.description: Rich, hearty stew from snapping turtle.

instructions.text: Parboil turtle meat 30 minutes; drain.
Brown meat and onion in pot.
Add broth, tomatoes, and bay leaf.
Simmer 1 hour until meat is tender.
Add potatoes; cook 30 minutes more. Season to taste.

notes: Turtle meat has seven distinct textures and flavors

recipes.title: Hog's Head Stew
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Meats and Small Game
recipes.description: Traditional use of hog's head meat in a rich stew.

instructions.text: Cover head with water; simmer until meat falls off bone, about 3 hours.
Remove meat from broth; pick meat from bones.
Return meat to broth; add vegetables and seasonings.
Simmer until vegetables are tender.
Serve hot with cornbread.

notes: Nothing was wasted in traditional hog butchering

recipes.title: Liver Pudding
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Meats and Small Game
recipes.description: Traditional Appalachian liver pudding (livermush).

instructions.text: Boil liver and pork scraps until very tender.
Grind or mash meat fine.
Return to cooking liquid; stir in cornmeal and seasonings.
Cook until thick, stirring constantly.
Pour into loaf pan; chill. Slice and fry to serve.

notes: Also known as livermush - a Carolina breakfast tradition

recipes.title: Brains and Eggs
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Meats and Small Game
recipes.description: Traditional breakfast of scrambled eggs with hog brains.

instructions.text: Soak brains in cold salted water 30 minutes; remove membrane.
Parboil brains 10 minutes; drain and chop.
Beat eggs with salt and pepper.
Melt butter in skillet; add brains and heat through.
Add eggs; scramble together until set.

notes: A delicacy at hog-killing time in Appalachia

recipes.title: Pickled Pig's Feet
recipes.source_note: Foxfire Americana Library - Meats and Small Game
recipes.description: Tangy preserved pig's feet in spiced brine.

instructions.text: Cover pig's feet with salted water; simmer 3-4 hours until tender.
Remove feet and pack into clean jars.
Boil vinegar, water, and spices together.
Pour hot brine over feet in jars.
Seal and refrigerate at least 1 week before eating.

notes: A traditional way to preserve meat without refrigeration

recipes.title: Squirrel Stew with Paprika and Greens
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Squirrel Stew with Paprika
recipes.description: A hearty Cajun-style squirrel stew with smoked sausage, paprika, greens and tomatoes.

instructions.text: Season squirrel pieces with salt and dust with flour.
Heat olive oil in a heavy Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Brown squirrels in batches without crowding. Set browned pieces aside.
Remove all squirrel from pot and add onions. Sauté 6-8 minutes until edges brown.
Add minced garlic and cook 1 minute. Stir in tomato paste and cook 2-3 minutes, stirring frequently.
Pour in white wine, vinegar, and approximately 1 quart water. Add savory, red pepper flakes, and paprika.
Add torn tomatoes and return squirrel to pot. Bring to simmer and cook approximately 90 minutes until meat falls from bones easily.
Remove squirrel pieces and pull meat from bones. Return meat to pot.
Add sliced sausage and greens; cook about 10 minutes until greens are tender (collards need 15-20 minutes).
Season to taste and serve with crusty bread.

notes: Chicken, turkey, or rabbit can substitute for squirrel
Better the next day like most stews

recipes.title: Cajun Turtle Sauce Piquante
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: A Cajun tomato-based stew with snapping turtle, one of the few Cajun dishes that commonly has tomato in it.

instructions.text: Make a blonde roux: Melt butter in a Dutch oven over medium heat. Add flour and cook, stirring constantly, until it turns the color of peanut butter (10-15 minutes). Do not let it get darker.
Add the holy trinity (onion, celery, bell pepper) and cook until softened, about 10 minutes.
Add garlic and cook 1 minute.
Add white wine and scrape up any browned bits.
Add crushed tomatoes, hot water, bay leaves, and Cajun seasoning. Stir well.
Add diced turtle meat. Bring to a simmer.
Cook gently for 1.5-2 hours until turtle is tender. The small dice makes tough turtle meat innocuous.
Season with salt, pepper, and hot sauce to taste.
Serve over white rice, garnished with green onions. Put hot sauce on the table.

notes: Turtle uses a blonde (peanut butter colored) roux and white wine, unlike dark meat which uses chocolate-colored roux and red wine
Alligator, frog legs, squirrel, or chicken thighs work as alternatives
Better the day after it's made

recipes.title: Creole Turtle Soup
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Classic New Orleans-style turtle soup with sherry and hard-boiled eggs.

instructions.text: Make a dark roux: Melt butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add flour and cook, stirring constantly, until it turns the color of milk chocolate (20-30 minutes).
Add onion, celery, and bell pepper. Cook until softened, about 10 minutes.
Add garlic and tomato paste. Cook 2 minutes.
Add crushed tomatoes, stock, sherry, Worcestershire, bay leaves, thyme, and cayenne.
Add turtle meat and bring to a simmer.
Simmer gently for 2 hours until turtle is very tender.
Remove bay leaves. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Serve in bowls, garnished with chopped hard-boiled eggs, thin lemon slices, and parsley. Pass extra sherry at the table.

notes: A Commander's Palace classic
Pass sherry at the table for diners to add more
Snapping turtle is traditional

recipes.title: Braised Squirrel Aurora (Spanish Style)
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Spanish-style braised squirrel with almonds and green olives.

instructions.text: Season squirrel pieces with salt and pepper.
Heat olive oil in a Dutch oven or braiser over medium-high heat. Brown squirrel pieces on all sides. Remove and set aside.
Add onion and cook until softened, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and cook 1 minute.
Add white wine and scrape up browned bits. Add stock, saffron if using, and bay leaf.
Return squirrel to pot. Add almonds and olives.
Cover and braise at a gentle simmer for 1-1.5 hours until squirrel is tender.
If using potatoes, add them in the last 30 minutes of cooking.
Remove bay leaf, adjust seasoning, and serve.

notes: Rabbit or chicken can substitute for squirrel
The almonds and olives are the defining flavors

recipes.title: Grilled Doves La Mancha
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Grilled Doves La Mancha
recipes.description: Spanish-style grilled doves with herbs and smoked paprika - the ultimate dove recipe.

instructions.text: Spatchcock the doves by cutting out the backbone and pressing flat.
Mix olive oil, paprika, garlic, thyme, rosemary, salt, pepper, and sherry vinegar to make a paste.
Coat doves thoroughly with the paste. Marinate at least 1 hour or overnight.
Heat grill to high. Clean and oil the grates.
Grill doves skin-side down first for 3-4 minutes until skin is crispy.
Flip and grill another 2-3 minutes. Breast meat should be pink (medium).
Rest 5 minutes before serving.

notes: Grilling is the best way to get crispy skin without overcooking the breast
Also works with pigeons, squab, teal, woodcock, rails, quail, or Cornish game hens
Serve medium (pink inside) - not well done

recipes.title: Hank's Dove Poppers
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: The most popular dove recipe in America - dove breasts with roasted garlic, poblano chiles, wrapped in bacon.

instructions.text: Mix cream cheese with mashed roasted garlic, diced poblano, and minced jalapeño. Season with salt and pepper.
Butterfly each dove breast if thick, or leave whole if small.
Place a spoonful of filling on each dove breast.
Roll up and wrap with half a slice of bacon. Secure with a toothpick.
Grill over medium-high heat, turning occasionally, until bacon is crispy and dove is cooked through but still pink inside, about 10-15 minutes.
Alternatively, bake at 400°F for 15-20 minutes.

notes: Different from traditional poppers with roasted garlic and poblano instead of just jalapeño and cheese
Can use duck, goose, quail, or pheasant breast

recipes.title: Wild Boar Sausage
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: A coarse, country-style wild boar sausage that highlights the flavor of the boar.

instructions.text: Cube meat and fat. Freeze for 30 minutes to make grinding easier.
Grind meat and fat together through a coarse plate (3/8 inch).
Mix ground meat with salt, pepper, sage, thyme, and garlic.
Add ice water and mix until the mixture becomes sticky and cohesive.
Fry a small test patty to check seasoning. Adjust if needed.
Stuff into soaked hog casings, twisting into 6-inch links.
Let rest uncovered in refrigerator overnight to dry slightly before cooking.

notes: Use 20-25% fat for best results
Wild boar fat can be softer - mixing with domestic pork fat helps
Can be used as bulk sausage without casings

recipes.title: Grilled Deer Heart with Peppers and Onions
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Grilled venison heart served with marinated peppers and onions - a celebration of the hunt.

instructions.text: Clean heart by trimming off fat, arteries, and silverskin. Slice into 1/2-inch steaks.
Mix olive oil, vinegar, garlic, rosemary, salt, and pepper.
Marinate heart slices for 30 minutes to 2 hours.
Grill peppers and onions over medium heat until charred and softened. Set aside.
Grill heart slices over high heat, 2-3 minutes per side for medium-rare.
Let rest 5 minutes. Slice against the grain and serve with peppers and onions.

notes: Works with elk, moose, antelope, or beef heart
Elk or moose heart feeds up to 6 people
Serve medium-rare to medium - overcooking makes it tough

recipes.title: Brunswick Stew
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Iconic Southern stew traditionally made with squirrel, though many meats work.

instructions.text: Render bacon in a large pot. Remove and set aside.
Brown meat pieces in bacon fat. Remove and set aside.
Sauté onion until softened.
Add stock, ham hock, and browned meat. Simmer 2 hours until meat is very tender.
Remove meat and ham hock. Shred all meat and discard bones.
Add potatoes, cook 15 minutes. Add beans and corn, cook 15 more minutes.
Add tomatoes, Worcestershire, hot sauce, vinegar, and brown sugar.
Return shredded meat to pot. Simmer 30 minutes, mashing some potatoes to thicken.
Season with salt and pepper. Serve with cornbread.

notes: Squirrel is traditional but chicken is common now
Virginia claims this stew originated there, Georgia disputes this
Stew should be thick enough to eat with a fork

recipes.title: Wild Hog BBQ (Pulled Pork)
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Slow-smoked wild hog shoulder for pulled pork - takes longer than domestic pork.

instructions.text: Mix dry rub ingredients (brown sugar through salt).
Coat shoulder with mustard, then apply rub liberally. Let sit overnight in refrigerator.
Set up smoker for 225-250°F. Use oak, hickory, or fruit wood.
Smoke shoulder fat-side up. Spritz with vinegar every hour after first 3 hours.
When internal temp reaches 165°F (usually 6-8 hours), wrap tightly in foil or butcher paper.
Continue cooking until internal temp reaches 200-205°F and probe slides in easily.
Rest wrapped for at least 1 hour.
Pull meat, discarding fat and bone. Mix with BBQ sauce or serve sauce on the side.

notes: Wild hog takes longer than domestic due to less fat
Internal temp of 200-205°F is key for proper texture
Can finish in 300°F oven if needed

recipes.title: Roast Snipe
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Simple roast snipe over a bed of sea beans - a rare treat with flavor all out of proportion to its size.
recipes.servings_yield: 2 servings as appetizer, or 1 as main

instructions.text: Preheat oven to 450°F.
Pat snipe dry and season inside and out with salt and pepper.
Rub softened butter over the birds and sprinkle with thyme.
Roast in hot oven for 12-15 minutes for medium-rare.
Rest 5 minutes before serving.
Serve over blanched sea beans or samphire if available.

notes: One snipe makes a great appetizer, four make a hearty meal
Snipe has intense flavor despite small size
Cook medium-rare to medium

recipes.title: Jesse's Hot Fried Snipe
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Southern-style fried snipe doused with a hot sauce, honey, butter and garlic glaze.

instructions.text: Soak split snipe in buttermilk for at least 30 minutes.
Mix flour with salt, pepper, and cayenne.
Heat oil to 350°F in a deep pan or fryer.
Dredge snipe in seasoned flour, shaking off excess.
Fry until golden and cooked through, about 4-5 minutes.
Meanwhile, melt butter with hot sauce, honey, and garlic.
Drain fried snipe and immediately toss with the hot butter sauce.
Serve immediately.

notes: Also works with doves and quail
From Jesse Griffiths' book Afield

recipes.title: Salmis of Snipe
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: A classic French snipe recipe where birds are roasted, sauce made from bones, served with mushrooms.

instructions.text: Roast snipe at 450°F for 10-12 minutes until medium-rare. Let rest.
Remove breasts and legs from carcasses. Set meat aside, keeping warm.
Chop carcasses and sauté in butter over high heat for 5 minutes.
Add shallots and mushrooms, cook until mushrooms release liquid.
Add wine, stock, thyme, and bay leaf. Simmer 30 minutes.
Strain sauce, pressing on solids. Return to pan and reduce by half.
Add Cognac and reserved mushrooms. Season with salt and pepper.
Arrange snipe pieces on toast points and spoon sauce over.

notes: Classic French technique called 'salmis'
The sauce from the bones is the star
Works with woodcock, dove, or squab

recipes.title: Roast Woodcock with Cumberland Sauce
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Classic roast woodcock with Cumberland sauce - the king of game birds.

instructions.text: Preheat oven to 450°F.
Season woodcock inside and out with salt and pepper. Rub with butter.
Roast for 15-18 minutes for medium-rare (internal 130°F).
Meanwhile, make Cumberland sauce: Heat currant jelly with port, citrus zest and juice, mustard, and ginger until combined.
If you saved the livers, mash them on toast as a base.
Rest woodcock 5 minutes, then serve on toast with Cumberland sauce.

notes: Many consider woodcock the king of game birds
Traditionally served on toast spread with the bird's liver
Cook medium-rare - the meat should be pink

recipes.title: Pan-Seared Woodcock with Mushrooms
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Simple pan-seared woodcock served with roasted mushrooms and Brussels sprouts.

instructions.text: Roast mushrooms and Brussels sprouts at 400°F with 2 tbsp butter until browned, about 20 minutes.
Season woodcock pieces with salt and pepper.
Heat remaining butter in a skillet over medium-high heat.
Sear woodcock breasts skin-side down for 2 minutes. Flip and cook 1-2 more minutes for medium-rare.
Remove breasts. Add legs and cook 4-5 minutes total.
Remove legs. Add shallot, cook 30 seconds. Add wine and thyme, scraping pan.
Serve woodcock over roasted vegetables with pan sauce.

notes: Breasts cook faster than legs - cook separately
Woodcock has a strong, gamey flavor in a good way

recipes.title: Pheasant with Mushrooms and Cream
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Pheasant with Mushrooms and Cream
recipes.description: Simple, homey pheasant breasts with fresh mushrooms, cream and brandy.

instructions.text: Season pheasant breasts with salt and pepper.
Heat butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat.
Sear pheasant breasts for 3-4 minutes per side until golden. Remove and keep warm.
Add shallots and mushrooms to pan. Cook until mushrooms are browned, about 5 minutes.
Add brandy and carefully ignite to burn off alcohol (or just let it reduce).
Add cream and tarragon. Simmer until sauce thickens slightly, about 5 minutes.
Return pheasant to pan, spooning sauce over. Cook 2-3 more minutes.
Slice pheasant and serve with mushroom cream sauce.

notes: Also works with grouse, chicken, or turkey breast
Don't overcook - pheasant dries out easily

recipes.title: Pickle-Brined Fried Pheasant
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Pheasant brined in pickle juice then fried - tangy, tender, and crispy.

instructions.text: Brine pheasant pieces in pickle juice for 4-24 hours in refrigerator.
Remove from brine and soak in buttermilk for 30 minutes.
Mix flour, cornstarch, salt, pepper, paprika, and garlic powder.
Heat oil to 325°F - lower than typical fried chicken to account for leaner meat.
Dredge pheasant pieces in flour mixture.
Fry in batches for 12-15 minutes, turning occasionally, until golden and cooked through.
Drain on wire rack and season with salt while hot.

notes: Lower frying temperature prevents drying out lean game birds
Also works great with grouse and partridge
The pickle brine adds flavor and tenderizes

recipes.title: Duck or Goose Confit
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: Classic French duck confit - legs slowly cooked in duck fat until meltingly tender.

instructions.text: Mix salt, pepper, thyme, bay leaves, and garlic. Rub generously over duck legs.
Place legs in a container, cover, and refrigerate 24-48 hours.
Rinse legs and pat dry thoroughly.
Preheat oven to 250°F.
Place legs in a single layer in an oven-safe pot. Cover completely with duck fat.
Cook uncovered for 3-4 hours until meat is very tender and pulls easily from bone.
Let cool in fat. Store submerged in fat in refrigerator for up to 3 months.
To serve, remove legs from fat and crisp skin in a hot skillet.

recipes.pan_size: Dutch oven or deep baking dish
notes: Skin-on specklebelly and Canada goose legs are the gold standard
Do NOT make confit from breasts - they become livery
Stored in fat, confit keeps for months

recipes.title: Goose Breast with Orange (Greek Style)
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Goose Breast with Orange
recipes.description: Duck l'orange with a Greek twist using ouzo - works beautifully with goose.

instructions.text: Score goose breast skin in a crosshatch pattern. Season with salt and pepper.
Place breasts skin-side down in a cold pan. Turn heat to medium.
Render fat slowly for 10-12 minutes until skin is very crispy.
Flip and cook 3-4 more minutes for medium-rare (130°F internal).
Remove breasts and rest. Pour off most fat.
Add orange juice, zest, ouzo, honey, and stock to pan. Reduce by half.
Remove from heat and whisk in cold butter to make glossy sauce.
Slice goose breast against the grain and serve with sauce.

notes: Start skin-side down in a COLD pan for crispiest skin
Goose and duck should be served medium-rare like steak
Ouzo adds anise flavor - substitute Pernod or skip if unavailable

recipes.title: German Rabbit Stew with Lemon
recipes.attribution: Hank Shaw / Hunter Angler Gardener Cook
recipes.description: A light, brothy German rabbit stew with lemon, bay leaves, capers and sour cream.

instructions.text: Season rabbit pieces with salt and pepper.
Brown rabbit in butter over medium-high heat. Remove and set aside.
Sauté onion until softened, about 5 minutes.
Add stock, wine, bay leaves, and lemon zest. Return rabbit to pot.
Simmer covered for 1-1.5 hours until rabbit is tender.
Remove rabbit. Add lemon juice and capers to broth.
Temper sour cream with a little hot broth, then stir into pot.
Return rabbit, garnish with parsley. Serve with roasted potatoes.

notes: Different from hasenpfeffer - this is light and brothy
Rabbits are mild white meat, hares are strongly flavored red meat
Knockout dish with roasted potatoes

recipes.title: Siberian Bear Pelmeni
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Russian dumplings traditionally made with bear meat
recipes.description: Traditional Siberian dumplings with bear meat and lots of onion. The original pelmeni were made by bear hunters and frozen in the snow for the trail.

instructions.text: Make the dough: Mix flour with egg yolks, buttermilk, and water. Knead until smooth. Let rest 30 minutes.
Make the filling: Combine ground bear meat with onion, garlic, salt pork, salt, and pepper. Mix well.
Roll dough thin and cut into 3-inch rounds.
Place a small spoonful of filling in center of each round.
Fold in half and pinch edges to seal, then bring corners together to form the classic pelmeni shape.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil.
Boil pelmeni for 6-8 minutes to ensure bear meat is fully cooked.
Serve with sour cream mixed with dill and black pepper.

notes: Use a lot of onion - it's a defining feature of these dumplings
Can substitute pork or beef for bear
Traditionally made with sourdough using whey

recipes.title: Chinese Red Braised Pork or Bear
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Classic Chinese dish adapted for wild game
recipes.description: Sweet-savory braised fatty meat with star anise and dark soy sauce. Works beautifully with fat wild pigs or bear belly.

instructions.text: Bring a large pot of water to boil. Boil the whole slab of belly for 5 minutes. Remove and let cool.
Cut the meat into 2-inch cubes.
Mix sugar with 3 tablespoons water until dissolved.
In a wok or Dutch oven, heat the sugar syrup over medium heat until it turns amber, about 5 minutes.
Add the par-cooked meat and turn to coat with the caramelized sugar.
Add garlic, ginger, and scallions. Stir for 1 minute.
Add both soy sauces, wine, star anise, and enough water to barely cover the meat.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer.
Simmer for 90 minutes for pork, up to 3 hours for wild hog or bear, until meat is very tender.
Serve over steamed jasmine rice.

notes: Dark soy sauce has a slight molasses sweetness different from regular soy
Wild game may take longer than domestic pork
Any fatty cut works - shoulder is also good

recipes.title: Bear Fat Buttermilk Biscuits
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Classic biscuits made with rendered bear fat
recipes.description: Classic buttermilk biscuits using bear fat instead of butter or lard. Bear fat makes exceptionally flaky pastry with no gamey flavor.

instructions.text: Preheat oven to 450°F.
Whisk together flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt in a bowl.
Add the cold bear fat and cut it into the flour with a fork or pastry cutter.
Work quickly so the fat doesn't melt. You're done when the mixture looks like little crumbly peas.
Pour in the buttermilk and stir just until dough comes together. It should be sticky but pull away from the sides.
Don't overwork the dough or biscuits will be tough.
Turn out onto floured surface, pat to 3/4-inch thickness.
Cut with a biscuit cutter and place on baking sheet.
Bake for 12-15 minutes until golden brown.

notes: Can substitute up to 1/2 cup acorn flour for variety
Use fresh rendered bear fat, not hydrogenated lard
Duck fat or lard work as substitutes

recipes.title: French Fried Frog Legs
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - French-style fried frog legs with butter sauce
recipes.description: Classic French preparation of frog legs, lightly fried in clarified butter and served with garlic parsley butter sauce.

instructions.text: Soak frog legs in milk in the refrigerator for 1 hour. (Skip for store-bought legs.)
Remove legs from milk, pat dry, and season with salt and pepper.
Dredge legs lightly in flour, shaking off excess.
Heat clarified butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat until you see a wisp of smoke (about 340°F).
Add frog legs and cook 3-4 minutes per side until golden brown and cooked through.
Remove legs to a warm platter.
Add regular butter to the pan, then garlic. Sauté 30 seconds.
Add parsley and lemon juice, swirl to combine.
Pour sauce over frog legs and serve immediately.

notes: Frog legs taste like a combination of chicken breast, shrimp, and crab
Use clarified butter to fry - higher smoke point
Good fresh ingredients are key - no wilty parsley

recipes.title: Chinese Stir-Fried Frog Legs
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - An amalgam of General Tso's, kung pao, and black bean styles
recipes.description: Battered and fried frog legs tossed in a sweet-spicy sauce with vegetables. A fusion of Chinese-American classics.

instructions.text: Whisk egg yolks with 2 tbsp soy sauce. Marinate frog legs while prepping other ingredients.
Mix sauce ingredients: chile bean sauce, 2 tbsp soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, stock, and 1 tbsp cornstarch.
Remove frog legs from marinade and dust with remaining cornstarch.
Heat oil to 350°F. Fry frog legs in batches until golden, 3-5 minutes. Drain.
Pour off all but 2 tbsp oil from wok.
Get wok very hot. Add garlic, ginger, and shallot. Stir-fry 30 seconds.
Add bamboo shoots, mushrooms, bell pepper, and fried frog legs. Stir-fry 2 minutes.
Add sauce, toss to coat. Cook until sauce thickens, 1-2 minutes.
Drizzle with sesame oil and serve over steamed rice.

notes: Best eaten with chopsticks - meat slides right off the bones
Wood ear mushrooms add meaty texture but can be omitted
Find frog legs in Asian market freezer sections

recipes.title: Roast Chukar or Partridge
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Brined and roasted small game birds
recipes.description: Simple brined and roasted chukar partridge. The overnight brine keeps these lean birds juicy and gives you wiggle room during roasting.

instructions.text: Make brine: Pour hot water over salt, stir to dissolve. Add bay leaf, thyme, rosemary, sage, and cloves. Cool to room temperature.
Submerge birds in brine, cover, and refrigerate up to 8 hours.
Remove birds from brine, pat dry. Let sit uncovered in fridge several hours to dry the skin, or at room temperature 20 minutes.
Preheat oven to 450°F.
Stuff each bird cavity with a lemon quarter. Lightly salt exterior.
Lay celery stalks in a cast-iron pan to keep birds off the bottom.
Place birds on celery and roast 20-25 minutes.
Check temperature - breast meat should be 150-155°F, no higher. Pink is good.
Rest 5 minutes before serving.

notes: Never let breast meat exceed 155°F or it will be dry
Works for quail, small grouse, and Cornish game hens too
Only for plucked birds - don't use this recipe if skinned

recipes.title: Grouse Soup with Wild Rice
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Forest flavors in a bowl
recipes.description: The essence of the forest in a bowl - grouse meat with wild rice, porcini mushrooms, and chestnuts or acorns.

instructions.text: Place grouse carcasses, dried mushrooms, onion, carrots, and celery in a large pot with broth.
Simmer for 1 hour to extract flavor.
Strain broth through a fine strainer lined with paper towel. You need 2-3 quarts.
Chop the rehydrated mushrooms and reserve.
Bring strained broth to a simmer. Add salt and wild rice.
Cook at a slow boil. True wild rice cooks in about 25 minutes; cultivated takes longer.
When rice is nearly done, add grouse meat, chestnuts, mushrooms, and greens.
Simmer 5 minutes more and serve.

notes: For non-hunters: use turkey or chicken thighs, cultivated wild rice, and chestnuts
