Real foraged wild rice cooks faster than cultivated
Save grouse carcasses in freezer until you have enough

recipes.title: Venison Steak Diane
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Classic sauce for venison medallions
recipes.description: Seared venison medallions with a rich brandy, mustard, and Worcestershire sauce. Named for Diana, goddess of the hunt.

instructions.text: Pat venison dry and season generously with salt and pepper. Let sit 10 minutes.
Melt 2 tbsp butter in a heavy pan over medium-high heat.
Sear venison, turning every minute, until nicely browned and medium-rare. Remove to rest.
Add remaining butter to pan with shallots and mushrooms. Sauté until starting to brown.
Add garlic and sauté 30 seconds.
Turn off heat and add brandy. Turn heat back to medium - this prevents flare-ups.
Cook until brandy is almost evaporated.
Add mustard, tomato paste, Worcestershire, and stock. Simmer 2 minutes.
Add cream if using. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Slice venison and serve with sauce. Garnish with parsley.

notes: Steak Diane originated with Escoffier and was named for the goddess of the hunt
Works with any venison - deer, elk, moose, caribou, antelope
Don't overcook venison - medium-rare is best

recipes.title: Roast Sharp-tailed Grouse with Rose Hip Glaze
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Prairies bird with prairies garnish
recipes.description: Sharp-tailed grouse roasted with a rose hip jelly glaze. The dark meat should be served pink, like doves.

instructions.text: Preheat oven to 450°F.
Season grouse inside and out with salt and pepper.
Mix rose hip jelly with butter and vinegar to make glaze.
Brush grouse liberally with glaze.
Roast for 15-20 minutes, basting with glaze halfway through.
Breast meat should be pink - about 135-140°F internal temperature.
Rest 5 minutes before serving.

notes: Sharp-tailed grouse are red meat and should be served pink like doves
Substitute currant jelly or crabapple jelly if no rose hip
From a cooking standpoint, these are essentially giant doves

recipes.title: Deviled Duck Hearts
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Adapted from Fergus Henderson's The Whole Beast
recipes.description: British-style deviled hearts dusted with mustard and cayenne, served with watercress. 'Deviled' means anything with mustard and cayenne.

instructions.text: Trim hearts: remove the top above the white fat ring (arterial tissue). Leave small hearts whole, halve larger ones.
Mix flour, dry mustard, cayenne, and salt together.
Dust hearts with the seasoned flour mixture.
Heat duck fat in a pan over medium-high heat.
Add hearts and sauté 3-4 minutes, shaking pan to let them roll around.
Add grated onion, Worcestershire sauce, and broth.
Scrape up browned bits and let sauce reduce to a glaze, about 3 minutes.
Stir in parsley and serve immediately with watercress and crusty bread.

notes: Works with any small hearts: chicken, pheasant, grouse, quail, turkey, rabbit
Teal hearts stay whole, goose hearts should be sliced
Adapted from Fergus Henderson's nose-to-tail cooking

recipes.title: Venison Liver and Onions
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Classic preparation with double-soak method
recipes.description: Deer liver and onions done right, with a double-soak method to tame any off-flavors. Best with livers from young animals.

instructions.text: First soak: Dissolve salt in water. Soak liver slices for 30 minutes.
Second soak: Drain and soak liver in milk for 1 hour or overnight.
Melt 2 tbsp butter in a large skillet over medium heat.
Add onions and cook slowly until caramelized, 15-20 minutes. Remove and keep warm.
Remove liver from milk, pat dry, and season with salt and pepper.
Dredge liver slices in flour, shaking off excess.
Add remaining butter to pan over medium-high heat.
Sear liver quickly, about 2 minutes per side for medium. Don't overcook.
Serve liver topped with caramelized onions and fresh thyme.

notes: Double soak (brine then dairy) removes off-flavors
Works with elk, pronghorn, caribou, or any large mammal liver
Best with livers from young animals

recipes.title: Braised Venison Tongue
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Slow braised deer or elk tongue
recipes.description: Tongue braised low and slow until tender, then peeled and sliced. Makes excellent tacos de lengua.

instructions.text: Place tongues in a pot with stock, vegetables, and aromatics.
Add enough water to cover if needed.
Bring to a simmer, cover, and place in 350°F oven.
Braise until a knife inserts easily, about 2-3 hours depending on size.
Let tongues cool in the braising liquid until cool enough to handle.
Peel the outer membrane off the tongues - it should slip off easily.
Slice and serve warm, or dice for tacos.
Strain and reserve braising liquid for reheating or as a sauce base.

notes: Peel the membrane when tongue is warm - it comes off easily
Great for tacos de lengua with cilantro and onion
Can be served cold sliced, or reheated in braising liquid

recipes.title: Peppered Dove Breasts (Doves au Poivre)
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - French classic adapted for dove
recipes.description: Dove breasts seared in butter with an easy pan sauce of shallots, brandy, cream, and peppercorns. Simple, fast, and delicious.

instructions.text: Salt dove breasts well and keep refrigerated until ready to cook.
Heat 3 tbsp butter in a skillet over medium-high heat.
Sear dove breasts 2 minutes on one side only. Remove to rest.
Add shallot to pan and sauté 1 minute.
Turn off heat and add brandy. Turn heat back to medium.
Add stock and both peppers. Simmer 2 minutes.
Add cream and simmer until slightly thickened.
Swirl in remaining 1 tbsp butter.
Spoon sauce over dove breasts and serve.

notes: Pepper is the dominant flavor - use freshly ground
Green peppercorns found near capers in most stores
Dove breast should be pink inside

recipes.title: Turkish Roast Pigeon with Bulgur
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Middle Eastern stuffed pigeon
recipes.description: Turkish-style roast pigeon stuffed with spiced bulgur wheat and walnuts. The Middle East cooks the best pigeon.

instructions.text: Brine pigeons: dissolve salt in water, submerge birds, refrigerate 6-12 hours.
Make stuffing: Bring stock to simmer with cinnamon, cardamom, allspice, and 1 tsp salt. Add bulgur, cover, simmer 15 minutes.
Meanwhile, heat oil and fry onions and walnuts until colored.
Combine cooked bulgur with onion-walnut mixture. Cool slightly, then add mint and lemon juice.
Remove pigeons from brine, pat dry, and stuff loosely with bulgur mixture.
Preheat oven to 350°F.
Place celery stalks in pan, lay pigeons breast-side down on celery. Roast 25 minutes.
Turn birds over and roast 10 more minutes.
Increase heat to 500°F and roast 10 minutes to brown and crisp.
Serve on remaining bulgur with lemon juice and fleur de sel.

notes: Brining keeps lean wild pigeons from drying out
Can substitute ptarmigan, sharp-tailed grouse, or Cornish hens
Goes well with raki or medium-bodied red wine

recipes.title: Pigeon Tortellini
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Stuffed pasta with ground pigeon
recipes.description: Morsels of pasta stuffed with ground pigeon, sweet wine, herbs, and roasted garlic, served with a juniper butter sauce.

instructions.text: Make filling: Mix ground pigeon with roasted garlic, wine, herbs, Parmesan, salt, pepper, and egg.
Cut pasta into 3-inch squares.
Place small spoonful of filling in center of each square.
Fold corner to corner to make triangle, pressing edges to seal.
Wrap around finger and pinch corners together to form tortellini shape.
Bring large pot of salted water to boil.
Meanwhile, make sauce: Melt butter with juniper berries, add stock, simmer 5 minutes.
Cook tortellini until they float, about 3-4 minutes.
Toss with juniper butter sauce and extra Parmesan.

notes: Can substitute dove, pheasant, or duck for pigeon
Juniper adds a piney, gin-like note to the butter
Can make tortellini ahead and freeze

recipes.title: Sichuan Crispy Fried Carp
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - When life gives you carp, think East
recipes.description: Chinese-style whole fried carp - crispy and delicious. Carp is prized in Asia, and this is an excellent way to prepare it.

instructions.text: Score the fish in a crosshatch pattern on both sides, cutting to the bone.
Pat fish very dry and dust heavily with cornstarch, getting into all the cuts.
Heat oil in wok or deep pot to 375°F.
Carefully lower fish into oil and fry until golden and crispy, about 8-10 minutes. Keep oil temperature up.
Remove fish to a platter.
Pour off all but 2 tbsp oil. Add ginger, garlic, chiles, and Sichuan peppercorns. Stir-fry 30 seconds.
Add wine, soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, and stock. Simmer 2 minutes.
Pour sauce over fish and top with green onions.

notes: Works with any whole fish that fits in a wok
Scoring helps the fish cook evenly and get crispy
Carp is prized in Asian cuisines

recipes.title: Catfish Étouffée (Smothered Catfish)
recipes.description: Cajun smothered catfish in a rich tomato and pepper sauce. A wonderful way to celebrate this fish.

instructions.text: Melt butter in a large skillet over medium heat.
Add onion, celery, and bell pepper. Sauté until soft, about 8 minutes.
Add garlic and sauté 1 minute.
Stir in flour and cook 2 minutes, stirring constantly.
Add tomato paste and tomatoes. Cook 3 minutes.
Pour in stock and add Cajun seasoning and cayenne. Simmer 10 minutes.
Add catfish chunks and simmer gently until fish is cooked, about 8-10 minutes.
Stir in green onions and parsley.
Serve over steamed rice.

notes: Can add small shrimp or crawfish 5 minutes before end
Don't stir too vigorously or fish will break up
Use any fresh catfish - wild or farmed

recipes.title: Wild Turkey Carnitas
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Braised and crisped turkey for tacos
recipes.description: The perfect solution for tough wild turkey legs. Braised until tender, then shredded and crisped in lard for tacos.

instructions.text: Place turkey pieces in a large Dutch oven with stock, onion, garlic, bay leaves, oregano, cumin, and salt.
Add enough water to cover the meat.
Bring to a simmer, then cook gently until meat is very tender - 90 minutes for domestic, up to 4 hours for old wild tom.
Remove turkey and let cool. Reserve cooking liquid.
Shred meat off the bones, discarding tendons and cartilage.
When ready to serve, heat lard in a large skillet over high heat.
Add shredded meat and let sit without stirring until one side is crispy and browned.
Stir and repeat if desired for more crispy bits.
Serve in warm tortillas with lime, onion, cilantro, and salsa.

notes: The shredded meat keeps for a week in the fridge before crisping
Also works with pheasant, old chicken, or guinea hen
Crisp only the portion you're serving

recipes.title: BBQ Turkey Legs with Maple-Bourbon Sauce
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Barbecued wild turkey thighs
recipes.description: Slow-smoked turkey legs with a homemade maple-bourbon barbecue sauce. Thighs work better than drumsticks since they have fewer tough tendons.

instructions.text: Coat turkey thighs with dry rub and refrigerate for at least 2 hours or overnight.
Make the sauce: Combine ketchup, maple syrup, bourbon, vinegar, Worcestershire, paprika, garlic powder, and cayenne in a saucepan. Simmer 10 minutes.
Set up smoker or grill for indirect heat at 275°F.
Smoke thighs until internal temperature reaches 165°F, about 2-3 hours.
During the last 30 minutes, brush with barbecue sauce every 10 minutes.
Let rest 10 minutes before serving with extra sauce.

notes: Thighs are preferred over drumsticks - fewer tendons
Can also be done in oven at 275°F with liquid smoke
Works with store-bought or wild turkey

recipes.title: Southwestern Turkey Leg Stew
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - New Mexican stew with chicos
recipes.description: A classic New Mexican stew with dried corn (chicos), chiles, and braised turkey legs. The perfect use for tough wild turkey drumsticks.

instructions.text: Soak chicos or posole in water overnight. Drain.
Toast dried chiles in a dry pan until fragrant. Cover with hot water and soak 20 minutes. Blend smooth.
In a large pot, brown turkey legs on all sides. Remove and set aside.
Sauté onion until soft, add garlic, cumin, and oregano.
Add chile puree, stock, corn, and turkey legs.
Simmer until turkey is fall-off-the-bone tender and corn is soft, 2-3 hours.
Remove turkey, shred meat, discard bones and tendons.
Return meat to pot. Season with salt.
Serve with lime, cilantro, and radishes.

notes: Chicos are dried roasted corn used in New Mexican cooking
Can substitute hominy if chicos unavailable
The long cooking time tenderizes even old wild turkey

recipes.title: Wild Turkey Gumbo
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Classic Louisiana gumbo with turkey
recipes.description: One of the great uses for turkey drumsticks - a rich gumbo with andouille sausage and seafood. Uses turkey legs, thighs, and wings.

instructions.text: Simmer turkey in stock until tender, 2-3 hours. Remove turkey, reserve stock. Shred meat when cool.
Make roux: Heat oil in a large pot over medium heat. Whisk in flour.
Cook roux, stirring constantly, until dark chocolate brown, 30-45 minutes.
Add onion, celery, and bell pepper (the 'trinity'). Cook 10 minutes.
Add garlic and cook 1 minute.
Add reserved stock, bay leaves, thyme, and cayenne. Simmer 30 minutes.
Add andouille sausage and cook 15 minutes.
Add okra if using and cook 10 minutes.
Add shredded turkey and shrimp. Cook until shrimp are pink, about 5 minutes.
Remove from heat, stir in filé powder if using. Top with green onions.
Serve over rice.

notes: Never boil gumbo after adding filé or it becomes stringy
Turkey breast doesn't work well - use dark meat
Can use any smoked sausage if andouille unavailable

recipes.title: Homemade Andouille Sausage
recipes.description: A heavily seasoned Cajun sausage, almost always smoked. Can be made with any meat - pork, venison, bear, or beef.

instructions.text: Chill meat and fat in freezer until very cold but not frozen, about 30 minutes.
Grind meat and fat through coarse die (6-7mm).
Mix ground meat with all seasonings and powdered milk.
Add ice water and mix thoroughly until the mixture is tacky and binds together.
Stuff into hog casings, twisting into 6-inch links.
Let sausages dry uncovered in refrigerator overnight.
Set up smoker with pecan or other hardwood at 175-200°F.
Smoke until internal temperature reaches 150°F, about 3-4 hours.
Fully cook before eating by grilling, pan-frying, or adding to gumbo.

notes: Can use venison, bear, beef, or any meat
Pecan is traditional wood for smoking andouille
Smoked sausages can be frozen after smoking and before final cooking

recipes.title: Louisiana Boudin
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Cajun rice and meat sausage
recipes.description: A cooked sausage with meat, liver, rice, and Cajun seasonings. A Louisiana favorite that's loosely stuffed into casings.

instructions.text: Place meat, liver, fat, onion, celery, pepper, garlic, and bay leaf in a pot. Cover with water.
Simmer until meat is very tender, about 1.5 hours. Reserve cooking liquid.
Remove bay leaf. Grind everything through coarse die.
Add ground mixture to a large bowl with salt and Cajun seasoning.
Add cooked rice, parsley, and green onions.
Add up to 4 cups reserved cooking liquid and mix 3-5 minutes until cohesive but still loose.
Stuff loosely into hog casings, twist into 8-inch links.
Poach in salted water at 165-170°F for 10 minutes.
Serve immediately, or grill until casing is crispy.

notes: Everything is cooked before stuffing - a 'cooked sausage'
Can also be formed into balls and fried (boudin balls)
Best grilled so casing gets crispy
Works with duck, turkey, venison, or pork

recipes.title: Country-Style Venison Sausage
recipes.source_note: From honest-food.net - Rich sausage with bay and garlic
recipes.description: A rich country-style venison sausage where ground bay leaves and garlic are the dominant flavors. Especially good for grilling.

instructions.text: Grind bay leaves to powder in a spice grinder.
Mix all seasonings together.
Grind very cold venison and fat through coarse die.
Add seasonings and ice water to ground meat.
Mix by hand or with paddle attachment until mixture is tacky, about 2 minutes.
Fry a small patty to test seasoning. Adjust salt if needed.
Stuff into hog casings, twisting into 5-6 inch links.
Refrigerate overnight uncovered to dry casings.
Grill, pan-fry, or use in other recipes.

notes: Keep meat and fat very cold for best texture
Bay leaves must be ground to powder - whole bay leaf bits are unpleasant
Especially good on the grill

recipes.title: Polish Duck Sausages
recipes.description: A fine-grained, almost emulsified sausage like a real Polish kielbasa, but with duck as the dominant meat. Snow goose would be perfect here too.

instructions.text: Chill all meat and fat in freezer until very firm but not frozen.
Grind meat and fat through fine die (4mm).
Put ground meat in mixer with paddle. Add all seasonings and powdered milk.
Mix on low while adding ice water. Continue until mixture becomes sticky and emulsified, about 5 minutes.
Stuff into hog casings, twisting into 6-inch links.
Poach in 170°F water until internal temperature reaches 150°F, about 45 minutes.
Chill in ice water to stop cooking.
Grill or pan-fry before serving.

notes: Fine grind and emulsification create the smooth kielbasa texture
Snow goose works perfectly
Marjoram is essential for Polish flavor

recipes.title: Appalachian Cottage Cheese
recipes.attribution: Foxfire 4 - Mrs. Harriet Echols & Mrs. Nora Garland
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian cottage cheese from Foxfire 4
recipes.description: Simple homemade cottage cheese from clabbered raw milk.

instructions.text: Pour raw milk into enamel or metal pan. Set in warm place to sour slowly - 1-2 days.
After milk clabbers, lift off cream and refrigerate.
Heat skimmed clabbered milk over low fire until it curdles.
Pour into colander or cheesecloth to drain several hours, or hang in flour sack overnight.
Work cheese with hands or spoon, squeezing out remaining water.
Sprinkle in salt to taste. Mix in some sour cream if desired.
Package and refrigerate. Keeps several weeks.

notes: Mrs. Nora Garland hung curdled milk in a clean flour sack overnight to drain.

recipes.title: Mrs. Earp's Quick Cooked Cheese
recipes.description: A quick cheese that can be eaten right away, cooked in a skillet until it forms a cake.

instructions.text: Let cream rise on whole milk, skim it off for butter making.
Add 2-3 tablespoons buttermilk per gallon of skimmed milk and let sit out 2 days to sour and clabber.
Refrigerate clabbered milk until ready to use.
Pour 2 gallons clabbered milk into pan and heat until a little hotter than lukewarm.
Pour into cloth-lined strainer. Gather corners and squeeze whey through, leaving curds.
Put curds in bowl, add salt and raw egg. Mix with hands.
Melt butter in large iron frying pan.
Add curds and keep turning over medium heat until all curds melt together into a cake.
Turn out into dish to cool. It will form a cake as it cools.

notes: Can be eaten right away or kept several days.
Gets firm enough to slice after drying somewhat.
Keeps about a week.

recipes.title: Fried Apple Pies
recipes.description: Individual hand pies filled with spiced cooked dried apples, fried until crispy.

instructions.text: Add small amount of water to dried apples and cook until tender.
Mash with fork. Add sugar and cinnamon or allspice to taste.
Make crust: Mix flour, 1/2 cup Crisco, and water like regular pie crust.
Divide dough into fist-sized balls. Roll each very thin into a circle.
Place cooked apples on one half. Fold crust over and press edges with fork.
Poke small holes with fork to let air escape.
Heat Crisco in large iron frying pan until enough to almost cover pies.
Fry pies until golden on both sides.

notes: Yellow apples make tastier pies.
Can be baked instead - spread melted butter on top for crisp crust.

recipes.title: Mrs. Reese's Block Cheese
recipes.source_note: Traditional Appalachian cheese-making from Foxfire 4, Vilas, North Carolina
recipes.description: Traditional rennet cheese pressed into firm blocks that keep well for a month or more.

instructions.text: Pour milk into a large pan and heat on wood stove until a little past lukewarm.
Remove from heat and add the dissolved rennet and color tablets.
Let sit 15-30 minutes until milk stiffens and becomes jellylike.
Cut with knife or spatula into tiny squares, also running spatula under surface as if cutting into layers.
Let sit briefly, then work mixture gently until broken into pieces about the size of corn kernels.
Return pan to stove and heat slowly until almost as hot as touch can stand (not boiling), stirring constantly.
Remove from heat and let sit 15-30 minutes to cool.
Strain through cheesecloth in colander. Let drip naturally (don't squeeze).
Return curds to pan, add salt, and massage in well.
Put into cheesecloth-lined press. Add weight in stages and leave overnight (12 hours).
Remove from press and dry in open air for one week, turning twice daily.

notes: Before rennet tablets, a small piece of dried cow stomach lining was used.
Cheese keeps well for a month or more.

recipes.title: Sassafras Jelly
recipes.description: A unique jelly made from sassafras root tea.

ingredients.prep_note: from 4 roots boiled in 1 gallon water 15-20 min

instructions.text: Make tea: Boil 4 sassafras roots in 1 gallon water for 15-20 minutes. Strain.
Mix Sure-Jell with 8 cups sassafras tea in large saucepan.
Bring quickly to a hard boil, stirring occasionally.
Add 8 cups sugar and bring to a full rolling boil.
Boil hard one minute, stirring constantly.
Skim off foam with metal spoon.
Pour at once into jelly jars and seal with paraffin.

notes: The stronger the tea, the stronger the jelly flavor.

recipes.title: Bleached Apple Pie
recipes.description: Apple pie made with sulfur-bleached dried apples that taste like fresh apples.

instructions.text: Place bleached apple pieces in uncooked pie crust.
Add butter, sugar, and cinnamon to taste.
Cover with pastry strips or second crust if preferred.
Bake at 350°F for 30-35 minutes or until crust is golden brown.

notes: Bleached apples taste remarkably like fresh apples.
Use minimal water when cooking - water brings back sulfur taste.

recipes.title: Cherry-Apple Salad Mold
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 352
recipes.description: A gelatin salad mold with cherries, apples, celery, and walnuts in cherry gelatin.

ingredients.item: frozen unsweetened pitted dark sweet cherries

instructions.text: Let cherries stand at room temperature while preparing gelatin mixture.
In a saucepan bring 1 1/2 cups apple cider to boiling; remove from heat. Add gelatin; stir till dissolved. Chill till partially set.
Halve partially thawed cherries. Stir cherries, applesauce, celery, and nuts into gelatin mixture.
Pour into a 3- or 3 1/2-cup mold. Chill till firm. Unmold onto a lettuce-lined plate, if desired.
For sauce, stir enough apple cider or apple juice (3 to 4 tablespoons) into cream cheese to make a sauce of spooning consistency. Pass sauce with salad.

recipes.title: Creamy Fruit Salad
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 352
recipes.description: A creamy gelatin salad with mandarin oranges, banana, and walnuts in a sour cream base.

instructions.text: Drain orange sections, reserving syrup. Add enough orange juice to syrup to measure 1 cup.
In a medium saucepan bring mixture to boiling. Remove from heat. Add gelatin; stir till dissolved.
Gradually stir about 1 cup of the hot mixture into eggs. Return mixture to saucepan. Cook and stir till nearly bubbly; reduce heat. Cook and stir for 1 to 2 minutes more, but do not boil.
Remove from heat. Add sour cream and cream cheese. Beat till smooth. Chill till partially set.
Fold in oranges, banana, and nuts. Transfer to a 10x6x2-inch dish. Chill till firm.

recipes.title: Berry Salad
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 352
recipes.description: A gelatin salad with strawberries and raspberries in strawberry or raspberry-flavored gelatin.

ingredients.item: cranberry juice cocktail or apple juice

instructions.text: Drain berries; reserve syrup from each. Dissolve gelatin in boiling water.
Stir in reserved syrup, cranberry juice cocktail or apple juice, and lemon juice.
Chill till partially set (the consistency of unbeaten egg whites). Fold in berries.
Pour into a 5- or 5 1/2-cup mold. Cover; chill till firm.
Unmold onto a plate lined with leaf lettuce.

recipes.title: Beef Bourguignonne
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 374
recipes.description: A classic French stew flavored with burgundy wine, mushrooms, and pearl onions.

ingredients.item: boneless beef chuck roast, cut into 3/4-inch cubes
pearl onions or frozen whole onions

instructions.text: In a large Dutch oven or kettle cook half of the meat in 1 tablespoon of the hot oil till meat is brown. Remove from pan and add remaining oil, remaining meat, the chopped onion, and garlic. Cook till meat is brown and onion is tender. Drain fat. Return all meat to Dutch oven.
Stir in burgundy, beef broth, bay leaves, thyme, marjoram, 1/2 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Bring to boiling; reduce heat. Cover and simmer for 45 minutes.
Add mushrooms, carrots, and pearl onions. Return to boiling; reduce heat. Cover and cook for 25 to 30 minutes more or till tender.
Combine flour and water. Stir into meat mixture. Cook and stir till thickened and bubbly. Cook and stir 1 minute more. Discard bay leaves.
Stir in bacon. Serve with noodles and, if desired, garnish with parsley.

notes: Crockery-cooker directions available in original source

recipes.title: Vegetable-Beef Soup
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 374
recipes.description: A hearty beef soup with vegetables including corn, tomatoes, potatoes, and green beans.

ingredients.item: fresh or frozen cut green beans

instructions.text: In a large Dutch oven or kettle combine meat, bay leaves, salt, oregano, marjoram, pepper, and 8 cups water. Bring to boiling; reduce heat. Cover and simmer for 2 hours. Remove meat.

When cool enough to handle, cut meat off bones and coarsely chop. Discard bones. Strain broth through a large sieve or colander lined with 2 layers of cheesecloth. Skim fat and return broth to kettle.
Stir in meat, corn, tomatoes, potatoes, beans, carrots, celery, and onion. Return to boiling; reduce heat. Cover and simmer about 30 minutes or till vegetables are crisp-tender. Discard bay leaves.

notes: Shortcut version: substitute 1 pound beef stew meat cut into 1/2-inch cubes for the beef shank crosscuts

recipes.title: Chili
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 376
recipes.description: Thick, hearty, and packed with flavor. A classic chili with ground beef, tomatoes, and kidney beans.

instructions.text: In a large saucepan cook ground beef, onion, green pepper, and garlic till meat is brown. Drain fat.
Stir in undrained tomatoes, kidney beans, tomato sauce, chili powder, basil, salt, and pepper.
Bring to boiling; reduce heat. Cover; simmer for 20 minutes.

notes: Microwave directions: In a 2-quart casserole combine beef, onion, green pepper, and garlic. Micro-cook, covered, on 100% power (high) for 6 to 9 minutes or till meat is no longer pink and vegetables are tender, stirring once. Drain. Stir in remaining ingredients. Cook, covered, on high for 9 to 11 minutes or till heated through, stirring twice.

recipes.title: Barley-Beef Soup
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 376
recipes.description: Hearty beef and barley soup with vegetables.

ingredients.item: beef or lamb stew meat, cut into 1-inch cubes
parsnips or potatoes, cut into 1/2-inch cubes

instructions.text: In a large Dutch oven brown half of the meat in hot oil. Drain fat. Add water, onion, celery, bouillon granules, garlic, rosemary, bay leaf, and 1/4 teaspoon pepper.
Bring to boiling; reduce heat. Cover; simmer for 1 hour for beef (45 minutes for lamb).
Stir in frozen vegetables, parsnips, undrained tomatoes, and barley. Return to boiling; reduce heat. Cover; simmer 15 minutes or till tender. Discard bay leaf.

notes: Substitute 1/4 cup pearl barley; add with water.

recipes.title: Mulligatawny
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 378
recipes.description: A curried chicken soup with vegetables, apple, and rice. Indian-inspired comfort food.

instructions.text: In a saucepan mix broth, undrained tomatoes, celery, apple, carrot, onion, parsley, curry powder, lemon juice, and 1/4 teaspoon pepper.
Bring to boiling; reduce heat. Cover; simmer 15 minutes, stirring often.
Stir in chicken; heat through. Serve with rice and, if desired, flaked coconut.

notes: Microwave directions: In a 2-quart casserole mix all ingredients but chicken and rice. Micro-cook, covered, on 100% power (high) for 12 to 15 minutes or till tender; stir once. Add chicken. Cook, uncovered, on high for 1 to 2 minutes more. Serve with rice.

recipes.title: Pork Kebabs
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 233
recipes.description: Partially freeze pork for easier slicing. Grilled pork with vegetables on skewers.

ingredients.item: fresh ears of corn, cut into 1-inch pieces
green sweet red pepper, cut into pieces

instructions.text: Cook corn in boiling water for 5 minutes. Drain.
On 4 long skewers alternately thread pork, corn, and pepper pieces.
Combine taco sauce and lime juice; set aside. Combine margarine and salt; brush onto kabobs.

Grill directly over medium-hot coals, turning and brushing with margarine mixture, for 15 to 18 minutes. Broil 4 to 5 inches from the heat for 15 to 18 minutes or till meat is no longer pink. Serve with taco sauce.

recipes.title: Pork Chow Mein
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 233
recipes.description: Classic Chinese-American stir-fry served over noodles.

instructions.text: In a large skillet brown half of the pork in hot oil. Brown remaining pork with onion rings and garlic. Return all pork to skillet.
Stir in undrained tomatoes, bouillon granules, thyme, and 1/4 teaspoon pepper.
Cover. Simmer 45 minutes or till tender.
Skim fat, if necessary. Combine flour and 1/4 cup cold water; stir into pork mixture. Cook and stir till thickened and bubbly. Cook and stir for 1 minute more. Serve over noodles.

recipes.description: Reference chart for cooking times of homemade and packaged pasta. Includes instructions for cooking pasta al dente and times for 40+ pasta shapes.

instructions.text: In a large saucepan or Dutch oven bring water (about 3 quarts for 4 to 8 ounces pasta) to boiling. If desired, add 1 teaspoon salt and 1 tablespoon olive oil. Add pasta a little at a time so water does not stop boiling. Cook for time specified, stirring occasionally. Test often for doneness near the end. Drain in a colander.

notes: If homemade pasta is dried or frozen, allow a few more minutes

recipes.title: Cheesy Chicken Kiev
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 304
recipes.description: A variation of Chicken Kiev with cheese instead of butter filling.

ingredients.item: whole large chicken breasts, skinned, boned, halved
caraway cheese, Gruyère, blue cheese, Camembert, Brie, or cheddar

instructions.text: Prepare as for Chicken Kiev, except substitute the cheese sticks for the butter in the chicken rolls.

recipes.title: Salad Greens Identification Guide
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 335

instructions.text: See visual guide for salad green identification. Combine two or more greens for flavor variety.

recipes.title: Beef-Asparagus Salads
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 336
recipes.description: A great way to use leftover beef. Main-dish salad with beef, asparagus, tomatoes, and mushrooms.

ingredients.item: dry sherry or red wine vinegar

instructions.text: For marinade, in a screw-top jar combine oil, lemon juice, sherry or vinegar, and lemon-pepper seasoning. Cover and shake well.
In a mixing bowl combine beef or turkey and onion. Add marinade. Toss lightly to coat. Let stand at room temperature for 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, cook asparagus in boiling salted water for 10 to 15 minutes or till nearly tender. Drain asparagus. Rinse with cold water. Let stand, covered with cold water.
Drain beef and onion, reserving 3 tablespoons of the marinade for Basil Mayonnaise.

For salads, line 4 salad plates with lettuce. Cut tomatoes in half and arrange around edge of each plate. Arrange one-fourth of the cucumber, mushrooms, asparagus spears, and beef mixture in center of each plate. Serve with Basil Mayonnaise.

notes: Basil Mayonnaise: Mix together 1/2 cup mayonnaise or salad dressing, 3 tablespoons reserved marinade, and 1 tablespoon snipped fresh basil or 1 teaspoon dried basil, crushed.

recipes.title: Marinated Steak Salads
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 336
recipes.description: The steak marinates in a tangy herb-flavored dressing after you cook it.

instructions.text: Slash fat edges of steak at 1-inch intervals, being careful not to cut into meat. Place steak on the unheated rack of a broiler pan. Broil 3 inches from the heat for 6 minutes. Turn steak. Broil to desired doneness (allow 6 to 9 minutes more for medium). Cool slightly; cut into thin slices. Place steak slices in a plastic bag; place bag in a bowl.
Cut any large artichoke hearts in half. Add artichoke hearts, cherry tomatoes, carrot, and green onions to the plastic bag. Set aside.

For marinade, in a screw-top jar combine olive oil, vinegar, lemon peel and juice, thyme, garlic salt, marjoram, and pepper. Cover and shake well. Pour marinade over steak and vegetables in the bag. Seal bag. Marinate in the refrigerator for 6 to 24 hours, turning bag occasionally.

For salad, toss together greens and mushrooms. Place greens and mushrooms on 4 salad plates. Drain steak and vegetables, reserving marinade, if desired. Arrange steak and vegetables over greens on plates. Drizzle with reserved marinade, if desired.

recipes.title: Cranberry Relish Ring
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 354
recipes.description: A festive cranberry gelatin mold with pineapple and orange.

instructions.text: Dissolve sugar and gelatins in boiling water. Add carbonated beverage and undrained pineapple.

Chill till partially set (the consistency of unbeaten egg whites). Using a food processor or food grinder with a coarse blade, grind unpeeled orange and cranberries. Fold cranberry mixture into gelatin.
Pour into a 6 1/2-cup ring mold or a 12x7 1/2x2-inch dish. Chill till firm.

notes: Shortcut Cranberry Relish Ring: Prepare as above, except reduce sugar to 1/4 cup and substitute two 10-ounce packages frozen cranberry-orange relish, thawed, for the ground orange and cranberries.

recipes.title: Frozen Black Cherry Cups
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 354
recipes.description: Frozen fruit salad cups with pineapple, cherries, banana, and pecans.

ingredients.item: medium banana, peeled and coarsely chopped

instructions.text: Combine pineapple, sour cream, yogurt, and lemon juice. Gently stir in cherries, banana, and pecans.
Spoon into 12 paper bake cups in muffin pans. Cover and freeze for 2 to 24 hours.
To serve, let stand at room temperature about 20 minutes to thaw slightly. Remove paper bake cups. Place on lettuce-lined salad plates.

recipes.title: Herbed Lamb Stew
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 375
recipes.description: A hearty lamb or pork stew with vegetables and sour cream.

ingredients.item: lamb or pork stew meat, cut into 3/4-inch cubes
dry red wine or beef broth

instructions.text: In a large saucepan brown meat, half at a time, in hot oil. Drain fat. Return all meat to pan. Add broth, wine, garlic, marjoram, bay leaf, 1/4 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 teaspoon pepper.

Bring to boiling; reduce heat. Cover; simmer 20 minutes or till nearly tender. Stir in potatoes, carrots, celery, and onion. Return to boiling; reduce heat. Cover; simmer about 30 minutes or till tender.
Discard bay leaf. Mix sour cream and flour. Stir 1/2 cup of the hot liquid into sour cream mixture. Return to pan. Cook and stir till bubbly. Cook and stir 1 minute.

notes: Microwave directions available in original source

recipes.title: Cioppino
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 379
recipes.description: California-born, this stew combines three kinds of fish and seafood in a tomato broth.

instructions.text: Thaw fish, if frozen. Cut fish into 1-inch pieces. In a large saucepan cook green pepper, onion, and garlic in hot oil till tender.
Add tomatoes, tomato sauce, wine, parsley, oregano, basil, salt, and dash pepper. Bring to boiling; reduce heat. Cover and simmer 20 minutes.
Add fish, undrained clams, and shrimp. Bring just to boiling; reduce heat. Cover and simmer 5 to 7 minutes or till fish flakes easily with a fork.

recipes.title: New England Clam Chowder
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 379
recipes.description: Serve this creamy chowder as a main dish or a side dish.
recipes.servings_yield: 4 main-dish servings or 6 to 8 side-dish servings

ingredients.item: shucked clams or two 6 1/2-ounce cans minced clams

instructions.text: Chop shucked clams, reserving juice; set clams aside. Strain clam juice to remove bits of shell. (Or, drain canned clams, reserving juice.) If necessary, add water to clam juice to equal 1 cup. Set clam-juice mixture aside.
In a large saucepan cook bacon till crisp. Remove bacon, reserving 1 tablespoon drippings. Drain bacon on paper towels; crumble. Set aside.

In the same saucepan combine reserved bacon drippings, reserved clam juice, potatoes, onion, bouillon granules, Worcestershire sauce, thyme, and pepper. Bring to boiling; reduce heat. Cover and simmer about 10 minutes or till potatoes are tender.

With the back of a fork, mash potatoes slightly against the side of the pan. Combine milk, cream, and flour till smooth. Add to potato mixture. Cook and stir till slightly thickened and bubbly. Stir in clams. Return to boiling; reduce heat. Cook 1 to 2 minutes more. Sprinkle each serving with some of the crumbled bacon.

notes: Fish Chowder: Prepare as above, except substitute 1 pound fresh or frozen fish steaks, cut 3/4 inch thick, for clams.

recipes.title: Ham and Bean Soup
recipes.source_note: Better Homes & Gardens New Cook Book, page 377
recipes.description: Classic ham and navy bean soup.

ingredients.item: smoked pork hocks or meaty ham bone

instructions.text: Rinse beans. In a large saucepan combine beans and water. Bring to boiling; reduce heat. Simmer for 2 minutes. Remove from heat. Cover and let stand for 1 hour. (Or, skip boiling the water and soak beans overnight in a covered pan.)

Drain and rinse beans. In the same pan combine beans, 4 cups fresh water, pork, celery, onion, thyme, salt, pepper, and bay leaf. Bring to boiling; reduce heat. Cover; simmer about 1 hour or till beans are tender.
Remove meat. When cool enough to handle, cut meat off bones and coarsely chop. Discard bones and bay leaf. Slightly mash beans in saucepan. Return the meat to saucepan. Heat through.

notes: Shortcut Ham and Bean Soup: Prepare as above, except omit dry beans. In a large saucepan combine 3 cups water, pork, celery, onion, thyme, salt, pepper, and bay leaf. Cover and simmer for 45 minutes. When cool enough to handle, cut meat off bones and coarsely chop. Discard bones and bay leaf. Return meat to saucepan. Stir in one 15-ounce can undrained navy or great northern beans. Heat through.

recipes.title: Directions for Selecting Meat (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), pages 32-33
recipes.description: Historical guide to selecting quality beef, mutton, lamb, veal, and pork from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: BEEF: The large stall-fed ox beef is the best. It has a coarse open grain and oily smoothness. Dent it with your finger and it will immediately rise again; if old, it will be rough and spongy, and the dent remain. Cow beef is less boned and generally more tender and juicy than the ox in America.
MUTTON: Grass-fed is good at two or three years old.
LAMB: If under six months is rich, and no danger of imposition; it may be known by its size.
VEAL: Is soon lost—great care therefore is necessary in purchasing. Veal brought to market in panniers, or in carriages, is to be preferred to that brought in bags and flouncing on a sweaty horse.
PORK: Is known by its size and whether properly fattened by its appearance.
Of almost every species of Animals, Birds and Fishes, the female is the tenderest, the richest flavored, and among poultry the soonest fattened.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: To Make the Best Bacon (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 32
recipes.description: Historical method for curing bacon from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: To each ham put one ounce saltpetre, one pint bay salt, one pint molasses.
Shake together 6 or 8 weeks, or when a large quantity is together, baste them with the liquor every day.
When taken out to dry, smoke three weeks with cobs or malt fumes.
To every ham may be added a cheek, if you stow away a barrel and not alter the composition, some add a shoulder.
For transportation or exportation, double the period of smoking.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Directions for Selecting Fish (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), pages 33-34
recipes.description: Historical guide to selecting quality fish from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: SALMON: The noblest and richest fish taken in fresh water—the largest are the best. They are unlike almost every other fish, are ameliorated by being 3 or 4 days out of water, if kept from heat and the moon (which has much more injurious effect than the sun).
In all great fish-markets, great fish-mongers strictly examine the gills—if the bright redness is exchanged for a low brown, they are stale.

SHAD: Contrary to the generally received opinion, are not so much richer flavored when first taken out of the water. A Shad 36 or 48 hours out of water may not cook so hard and solid, yet give a higher relished flavor to the taste.

Every species generally of salt water Fish are best fresh from the water, though Hannah Hill, Black Fish, Lobster, Oyster, Flounder, Bass, Cod, Haddock, and Eel, with many others, may be transported by land many miles, find a good market, and retain a good relish.
Fresh gills, full bright eyes, moist fins and tails are denotements of their being fresh caught; if they are soft, it's certain they are stale.
SALMON TROUT: They are best when caught under a fall or cataract—the waters are much colder at the foot of a fall than at the head; Trout choose those waters.
PERCH AND ROACH: Noble pan fish, the deeper the water from whence taken, the finer are their flavors; if taken from shallow water with muddy bottoms, they are impregnated therewith and are unsavory.
EELS: Though taken from muddy bottoms, are best to jump in the pan.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Directions for Selecting Poultry (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), pages 35-36
recipes.description: Historical guide to selecting quality poultry and game birds from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: The female in almost every instance is preferable to the male, and peculiarly so in the PEACOCK, which though beautifully plumaged, is tough, hard, stringy, and even indelicious—while the Pea Hen is exactly otherwise, and the queen of all birds.
TURKEY: Hen turkey is higher and richer flavored, easier fattened and plumper—they are no odds in market.
CHICKENS: Of either kind are good, and the yellow legged the best, and their taste the sweetest.
CAPONS: If young are good, are known by short spurs and smooth legs.

All birds are known, whether fresh killed or stale, by a tight vent in the former, and a loose open vent if old or stale; their smell denotes their goodness; speckled rough legs denote age, while smooth legs and combs prove them young.

A GOOSE: If young, the bill will be yellow, and will have but few hairs, the bones will crack easily; but if old, the contrary—the bill will be red, and the pads still redder; the joints stiff and difficultly disjointed; if young, otherwise choose one not very fleshy on the breast, but fat in the rump.
DUCKS: Are similar to geese. WILD DUCKS have redder pads, and smaller than the tame ones, otherwise are like the goose or tame duck, or to be chosen by the same rules.
WOOD COCKS: Ought to be thick, fat and flesh firm, the nose dry, and throat clear.
SNIPES: If young and fat, have full veins under the wing, and are small in the veins, otherwise like the Woodcock.
PARTRIDGES: If young, will have black bills, yellowish legs; if old, the legs look bluish; if old or stale, it may be perceived by smelling at their mouths.

PIGEONS: Young have light red legs, and the flesh of a colour, and prick easily—old have red legs, blackish in parts, more hairs, plumper and loose vents—so also of grey or green Plover, Black Birds, Thrash, Lark, and wild Fowl in general.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Directions for Selecting Vegetables (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), pages 37-42
recipes.description: Historical guide to selecting quality vegetables from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: POTATOES: Take rank for universal use, profit and easy acquirement. The smooth skin, known by the name of How's Potatoe, is the most mealy and richest flavored; the yellow rusticoat next best; the red and red rusticoat are tolerable. Those cultivated from imported seed on sandy or dry loomy lands are best for table use. All potatoes should be dug before the rainy seasons in the fall, well dried in the sun, kept from frost and dampness during the winter.
ONIONS: The Madeira white is best in market, esteemed softer flavored and not so fiery, but the high red, round hard onions are the best; if you consult cheapness, the largest are best.
BEETS: Grow on any ground, but best on loom or light gravel grounds; the red is the richest and best approved; the white has a fickish sweetness which is disliked by many.

PARSNIPS: Are a valuable root, cultivated best in rich old grounds, and doubly deep plowed, late sown. They are richer flavored when plowed out of the ground in April, having stood out during the winter.

CARROTS: Are managed as it respects plowing and rich ground, similarly to Parsnips. The yellow are better than the orange or red; middling sized, a foot long and two inches thick at the top end, are better than over grown ones.
ASPARAGUS: The mode of cultivation belongs to gardening; the largest is best, the growth of a day sufficient, six inches long, and cut just above the ground.
LETTUCE: Is of various kinds; the purple spotted leaf is generally the tenderest, and free from bitter—Your taste must guide your market.
CABBAGE: They are so multifarious that requires a page. Note, all Cabbages have a higher relish that grow on new unmatured grounds.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Herbs Useful in Cookery (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 43
recipes.description: Historical guide to culinary herbs and their uses from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: THYME: Is good in soups and stuffings.
SWEET MARJORAM: Is used in Turkeys.
SUMMER SAVORY: Ditto, and in Sausages and salted Beef, and legs of Pork.
SAGE: Is used in Cheese and Pork, but not generally approved.
PARSLEY: Good in soups, and to garnish roast Beef, excellent with bread and butter in the spring.
PENNY ROYAL: Is a high aromatic, although a spontaneous herb in old ploughed fields, yet might be more generally cultivated in gardens, and used in cookery and medicines.
SWEET THYME: Is most useful and best approved in cookery.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: To Roast Beef (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 44
recipes.description: Historical method for roasting beef from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: The general rules are, to have a brisk hot fire, to hang down rather than to spit, to baste with salt and water.
Allow one quarter of an hour to every pound of beef, though tender beef will require less, while old tough beef will require more roasting.
Pricking with a fork will determine whether done or not; rare done is the healthiest and the taste of this age.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: To Roast Mutton (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 45
recipes.description: Historical method for roasting mutton from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: If a breast let it be cauled; if a leg, shuffed or not; let it be done more gently than beef, and done more.
The chine, saddle or leg require more fire and longer time than the breast.
Garnish with scraped horseradish, and serve with potatoes, beans, colliflowers, water-cresses, or boiled onion, caper sauce, mashed turnip, or lettuce.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: To Stuff and Roast a Turkey (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), pages 45-46
recipes.description: Historical recipe for stuffed roast turkey from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: Grate a wheat loaf, one quarter of a pound butter, one quarter of a pound salt pork, finely chopped, 2 eggs, a little sweet marjoram, summer savory, parsley and sage, pepper and salt (if the pork be not sufficient), fill the bird and sew up.
Hang down to a steady solid fire, basting frequently with salt and water, and roast until a steam emits from the breast.
Put one third of a pound of butter into the gravy, dust flour over the bird and baste with the gravy.
Serve up with boiled onions and cranberry sauce, mangoes, pickles or celery.
The same will answer for all Wild Fowl. Water Fowls require onions.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Johny Cake, or Hoe Cake (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 61
recipes.description: America's original Johnny Cake recipe from the first American cookbook.

instructions.text: Scald 1 pint of milk and put to 3 pints of Indian meal, and half pint of flour—bake before the fire.
Or scald with milk two thirds of the Indian meal, or wet two thirds with boiling water, add salt, molasses and shortening, work up with cold water pretty stiff, and bake as above.

notes: This is one of the earliest published recipes for Johnny Cake, a quintessentially American bread.
From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook.

recipes.title: Indian Slapjack (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 61
recipes.description: Early American pancake recipe from the first American cookbook.

instructions.text: One quart of milk, 1 pint of Indian meal, 4 eggs, 4 spoons of flour, little salt, beat together.
Baked on griddles, or fry in a dry pan, or baked in a pan which has been rubbed with suet, lard or butter.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Pompkin Pudding No. 1 (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 55
recipes.description: One of the earliest published pumpkin pie recipes from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: One quart stewed and strained pumpkin, 3 pints cream, 9 beaten eggs, sugar, mace, nutmeg and ginger.
Laid into paste No. 7 or 3, and with a dough spur, cross and chequer it.
Bake in dishes three quarters of an hour.

notes: This is one of the earliest published pumpkin pie recipes in America.
The word 'pompkin' was common spelling in 1796.
From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook.

recipes.title: Pompkin Pudding No. 2 (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 55
recipes.description: A simpler pumpkin pie variation from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: One quart of milk, 1 pint pumpkin, 4 eggs, molasses, allspice and ginger in a crust.
Bake 1 hour.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Apple Pie (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 52
recipes.description: Traditional apple pie recipe from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: Stew and strain the apples.
To every three pints, grate the peel of a fresh lemon, add cinnamon, mace, rose-water and sugar to your taste.
Bake in paste No. 3.
Every species of fruit such as peas, plums, raspberries, black berries may be only sweetened, without spices—and bake in paste No. 3.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: A Nice Indian Pudding No. 1 (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 53
recipes.description: Traditional Indian pudding (cornmeal pudding) from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: 3 pints scalded milk, 7 spoons fine Indian meal, stir well together while hot, let stand till cooled.
Add 7 eggs, half pound raisins, 4 ounces butter, spice and sugar.
Bake one and half hour.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: A Rice Pudding No. 1 (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 52
recipes.description: Traditional rice pudding from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: One quarter of a pound rice, a stick of cinnamon, to a quart of milk (stirred often to keep from burning).
Boil quick, cool and add half a nutmeg, 4 spoons rose-water, 8 eggs.
Butter or puff paste a dish and pour the above composition into it.
Bake one and half hour.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Cookies (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 63
recipes.description: One of the earliest published cookie recipes in America, from the first American cookbook.

ingredients.prep_note: boiled slowly in half pint water

instructions.text: One pound sugar boiled slowly in half pint water, scum well and cool.
Add two tea spoons pearl ash dissolved in milk, then two and half pounds flour, rub in 4 ounces butter, and two large spoons of finely powdered coriander seed, wet with above.
Make roles half an inch thick and cut to the shape you please.
Bake fifteen or twenty minutes in a slack oven—good three weeks.

notes: This is one of the earliest published cookie recipes in America.
Pearl ash (potassium carbonate) was an early leavening agent.
From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook.

recipes.title: Christmas Cookey (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 63
recipes.description: Historic Christmas cookie recipe from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: To three pound flour, sprinkle a tea cup of fine powdered coriander seed, rub in one pound butter.
Add one and half pound sugar, dissolve three tea spoons of pearl ash in a tea cup of milk.
Kneed all together well, roll three quarters of an inch thick, and cut or stamp into shape and size you please.
Bake slowly fifteen or twenty minutes; though hard and dry at first, if put into an earthern pot, and dry cellar, or damp room, they will be finer, softer and better when six months old.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Molasses Gingerbread (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 64
recipes.description: Traditional molasses gingerbread from America's first cookbook.

ingredients.prep_note: in summer rub in the butter, if in winter warm the butter and molasses

instructions.text: One table spoon of cinnamon, some coriander or allspice, put to four tea spoons pearl ash dissolved in half pint water.
Add four pound flour, one quart molasses, four ounces butter (if in summer rub in the butter, if in winter warm the butter and molasses and pour to the spiced flour).
Knead well 'till stiff, the more the better, the lighter and whiter it will be.
Bake brisk fifteen minutes; don't scorch.
Before it is put in, wash it with whites and sugar beat together.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Pound Cake (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 64
recipes.description: Traditional pound cake from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: One pound sugar, one pound butter, one pound flour, one pound or ten eggs.
Add rose water one gill, spices to your taste.
Watch it well, it will bake in a slow oven in 15 minutes.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: For Brewing Spruce Beer (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 75
recipes.description: Historic spruce beer recipe from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: Take four ounces of hops, let them boil half an hour in one gallon of water, strain the hop water.
Then add sixteen gallons of warm water, two gallons of molasses, eight ounces of essence of spruce dissolved in one quart of water.
Put it in a clean cask, then shake it well together, add half a pint of emptins (yeast).
Then let it stand and work one week. If very warm weather less time will do.
When it is drawn off to bottle, add one spoonful of molasses to every bottle.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Emptins (Homemade Yeast) (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 76
recipes.description: Historic recipe for making emptins (homemade yeast) from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: Take a handful of hops and about three quarts of water, let it boil about fifteen minutes.
Then make a thickening as you do for starch, strain the liquor.
When cold put a little emptins (yeast) to work them.
They will keep well corked in a bottle five or six weeks.

notes: Emptins was the 18th century term for homemade yeast.
From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook.

recipes.title: Glossary of 18th Century Cooking Terms (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), pages 79-80
recipes.description: Glossary of historical cooking terms from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: AMBER GUM: Probably ambergris, the wax-like secretion of the sperm whale, now used in perfumery, formerly in cookery.
BELL-METAL: The metallic substance of which bells are made.
BLADDER AND LEATHER: Pieces of each substance to be tied over the mouths of jars and bottles to secure the contents against air.
BULLACE: A small wild or semi-domesticated plum.
CALAVANCE (CALIVANSE): The name for certain varieties of pulse; here, an early variety of bean.
CALIPASH: That part of the turtle adjoining the upper shell.
CALIPEE: That part of the turtle adjoining the lower shell.
CAUL: An enveloping membrane.
CHINE: A 'joint' made up of part of the backbone and adjoining flesh.
COB: Corn cob.
DO.: Abbreviation for ditto.
EMPTINS: Semiliquid prepared yeast.
FAIR: (of water) clean; pure.
FROST GRAPE: A native American species, also called 'chicken grape'.
FROWY, FROUGHY: Stale; sour; musty.
FRUMENTY: Hulled wheat cooked in milk and seasoned with spice, sugar, etc.
GALLIPOT: A small earthen pot.
HASLET, HARSLET (HEARTSLET): Edible entrails; liver, heart, etc.
JAGGING IRON or DOUGHSPUR: An instrument used for ornamenting pastry, in the form of a toothed wheel set in a handle.
JUMP IN THE PAN: A characteristic action of eels while in the process of cooking.
LADE: To transfer as with a ladle or scoop.
MANGO: A pickled green melon stuffed with various condiments.
NEAT'S FOOT: The foot of an ox.
ORANGE FLOWER WATER: A liquid distilled from orange blossoms.
PANNIKIN: A small metal vessel.
PEARLASH: A salt obtained from the ashes of plants (potassium carbonate, an early leavening agent).
PIPPIN: A variety of apple.
Q.S. (QUANTUM SUFFICIT): As much as suffices.
RACE: A root (as in 'a race of ginger').
RUN OUT or DEPRECIATE: To decline in quality with each planting.
SCUM: To skim.
SYLLABUB, SILLABUB: A mixture of milk or cream with wine, cider, or other acid, usually whipped to a froth.
WALLOP: A bubbling motion made by rapidly boiling water, hence the duration of one such motion used as a measure of time in cooking.

recipes.title: For Preserving Quinces (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), pages 66-67
recipes.description: Historic quince preserving recipe from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: Take a peck of Quinces, pare them, take out the core with a sharp knife.
If you wish to have them whole, boil parings and cores with two pound frost grapes in 3 quarts water, boil the liquor an hour and an half, or till it is thick.
Strain it through a coarse hair sieve, add one and a quarter pound sugar to every pound of quince.
Put the sugar into the syrup, scald and skim it till it is clear.
Put the quinces into the syrup, hang them over a gentle fire for five hours, then put them in a stone pot for use, set them in a dry cool place.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: To Pickle Cucumbers (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), pages 73-74
recipes.description: Historic cucumber pickle recipe from America's first cookbook.

ingredients.prep_note: small, fresh gathered, free from spots
for brine, strong enough to bear an egg

instructions.text: Let your cucumbers be small, fresh gathered, and free from spots.
Then make a pickle of salt and water, strong enough to bear an egg.
Boil the pickle and skim it well, and then pour it upon your cucumbers, and stive them down for twenty four hours.
Then strain them out into a cullender, and dry them well with a cloth.
Take the best white wine vinegar, with cloves, sliced mace, nutmeg, white pepper corns, long pepper, and races of ginger (as much as you please), boil them up together.

Then clap the cucumbers in, with a few vine leaves, and a little salt, and as soon as they begin to turn their colour, put them into jars, stive them down close, and when cold, tie on a bladder and leather.

notes: From American Cookery (1796), the first American cookbook. Language updated from 18th century spelling.

recipes.title: Currant Jelly (1796)
recipes.source_note: American Cookery by Amelia Simmons (1796), page 71
recipes.description: Historic currant jelly recipe from America's first cookbook.

instructions.text: Having stripped the currants from the stalks, put them in a stone jar, stop it close.
Set it in a kettle of boiling water, half way the jar, let it boil half an hour.
Take it out and strain the juice through a coarse hair sieve.
To a pint of juice put a pound of sugar, set it over a fine quick fire in a preserving pan, or a bell-metal skillet.
Keep stirring it all the time till the sugar be melted, then skim the scum off as fast as it rises.
When the jelly is very clear and fine, pour it into earthen or china cups, when cold, cut white papers just the bigness of the top of the pot, and lay on the jelly.
Dip those papers in brandy, then cover the top of the pot and prick it full of holes, set it in a dry place; you may put some into glasses for present use.

recipes.title: Spicy Meatballs
recipes.description: Sweet and tangy meatballs with a homemade BBQ-style sauce, perfect for slow cooking.

instructions.text: Mix ground beef, crumbled sausage, stuffing mix, eggs, onion flakes, and enough milk to moisten. Form into meatballs.
Bake meatballs until browned.
For sauce: Combine 1 cup sugar, 1/2 cup vinegar, 1/4 cup water, and 1 tsp paprika. Boil together 5 minutes.
Mix 2 tsp cornstarch in 1 tbsp cold water. Add to sauce and cook until clear, remove from heat.
Add BBQ sauce to taste for basting.
Simmer meatballs in sauce for 1/2 hour, or use crock pot.

notes: HANDWRITTEN FAMILY RECIPE - PRESERVE IMAGE
Can be made in crock pot for convenience
